blocks.h: A MADNESS WE KEPT WARM
Roya Publication No. 117
by Chew Z
THE BOOK BEFORE
Each of these books stands on its own, and if this is where you have come in, you have missed nothing you need. The one before this was about a man who went home.

He was past fifty, a careful man who had spent his working life bringing faded photographs and ruined old films back from the edge of nothing — a restorer of other people’s pasts, which is a strange trade for a man who had walked away from his own as young as he could. He had a mother, very old now, in the house on the California hillside he had grown up in and left. Word reached him that she was slipping: that her mind had come loose from the present, that she wandered in the garden and spoke to people who were not there, that she was, the word everyone used, going. So he went back, to sit with her at the end, in the overgrown garden she had never once in fifty years let anyone touch.

What he found was not what the word had promised. His mother was somewhere, all right — but not nowhere, and not simply lost. There was a shape to her wandering, a reason folded into the wild green of that garden, a thing she had been tending in plain sight for half a century that he had been too far away, and too afraid, to see. The distance between them, he began to understand, had never been the ordinary distance of a son who leaves. It had been built, on purpose, and kept.
That is all I will tell you, because the rest is that book’s to keep. This one is about something else, and someone else, three thousand miles east, in a dying town in the mountains.
SYNOPSIS

Clare and Daniel have been married most of their lives, and they are writers — two people who met over a sentence and have spent the thirty years since putting the world into words, badly paid and perfectly matched. The city they built that life in has grown too expensive to go on writing in, so they do a brave and foolish thing: they sell what they have and buy a cheap, beautiful house at the end of the world, a dying coal town in the West Virginia mountains, to write at last the second books that would not come.

For almost two years, in the gold light and the quiet, it works. They are happy. The work returns, better than it has ever been. And then, on an ordinary spring night, coming home over the mountain, a deer steps into the road.
What the hospital sends them home with, for the long mending and the pain that will not fully leave, comes into the house looking exactly like mercy.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
A word before you begin, because this one asks for it.

This is a book about the poppy, and about the long warm road it has walked beside us for ten thousand years, and the thing at the far end of that road that is still, as I write, taking more people every year than the last. It does not look away from where the road ends. If you have lost someone down it, parts of this will be hard, and I would rather say so now.

Alder is invented; there is no such town in West Virginia, and Clare and Daniel never lived. But the road that runs through the book is real — the accident, the amber bottle, the kind tired doctor, the staircase down, the town where it was in half the houses — and it is the true shape of what happened to a great many real people, and is happening still.

The title is an old idea in plain clothes. Doctors have a name for a shared madness — a delusion two people who love each other hold up between them, each keeping it warm in the other, so that neither can set it down alone. This is a book about two such people, and the warm thing they kept between them all the way down, and how the very closeness that saved them was also the thing that would not let them go.

One last thing, flatly, with no wink in it. Nowhere in this book is there a how: I have named the danger everywhere and the method nowhere, on purpose. And if you take from these pages that the warmth was worth it, you have read a different book than the one I wrote. The warmth was a counterfeit and a thief. What was worth it — if anything in that ruin was — is a thing the one who lived to tell it argues with herself to the last page and never quite wins, and I have left it unfinished.
Chew Z
I. THE GOOD YEARS
There are two stacks of notebooks on the desk in front of me, and one of them is still his.

Mine are on the left, and they are the cheap kind, the ones you buy in a plastic sleeve of five at the drugstore, because for a long time that was what we could afford and then for a longer time it was what we were used to. His are on the right. His were always nicer. He would not write in anything cheap; he said a sentence could tell what you had bought to keep it in, which was the kind of thing he said, and which I used to think was a pose and have since decided was simply true. His are cloth over board, dark blue and dark green and one the color of a brown egg, and the spines are soft now from being opened, and his handwriting is inside them, going a little downhill the way it always did on the right-hand page, as if the words were tired and leaning toward the gutter to rest.

I am sixty-one years old and I have been clean for ten years, and I am writing this at the same desk where we were going to write the books that were going to change our lives, in the same house, in the town we moved to on purpose, which is a thing I still cannot entirely explain to people, that we chose it, that we drove toward it with the windows down and the radio on and thought there, that one, that’s where the good part starts.

We were right, is the thing nobody wants me to say. The good part did start there. I just didn’t know yet that the word good was going to have to stretch to cover everything that came, the way a single sheet gets pulled up over two people and never quite reaches both, and you spend the whole night, half asleep, tugging it one way and the other, trying to keep you both warm under the one thing you have.

This is the book we were supposed to write. The second one. The one that wouldn’t come. It took me nine years and his death to find out what it was about, and it turns out it was about us, which is the one subject we were both always too proud and too frightened to touch. I am writing it out of both of us, because that is the only honest way I know to tell it: me now, at the desk, an old woman with good light and a cold cup of coffee; and Daniel then, in the blue notebook and the green one, saying it the way he said it, which was always better than the way I say it, and I have stopped minding that. I minded it for thirty years. I don’t anymore. There is nobody left to lose to.
So. Both of us. Here is how it was good.
We met over a sentence, which is the most us thing that ever happened to us, and we fought about it for an hour, and the fight was the beginning of everything.

It was a workshop, a seminar room with bad chairs, the fall I was twenty-four. There were eleven of us and a famous teacher who mostly slept behind his glasses, and we went around the table taking a story apart the way you do at that age, cruelly and joyfully, because tearing a thing down is how the young prove they could build one. The story was mine. I had written a sentence I was in love with — I won’t tell you what it was, it was terrible, it had a semicolon in it doing work no semicolon has ever been strong enough to do — and the room was being kind about it, which is to say they were killing it softly, and then a man at the end of the table whom I had not spoken to all semester said, “No, that sentence is the only honest thing in the whole story, you should throw out the story and keep the sentence.”

That was Daniel. He was wrong about the story and right about the sentence, and I hated him for about forty minutes and then I didn’t, and we went and got coffee that neither of us could afford and talked until the place closed and then walked until it got light, and I have told that story so many times that I no longer know which parts are true. But that part is. He read me the first time by the one sentence I had tried hardest to hide, and he liked me for exactly the thing I was most ashamed of, and if you want to know why a marriage lasts thirty years through everything ours went through, it is not more complicated than that. He was the one person who looked at the part of me I kept covered and said, that, keep that, that’s the good one.

We were broke in the way that only the young can be broke and enjoy it. We had a one-room apartment over a dry cleaner and the whole place smelled of steam and clean cotton, and we wrote at the same small table facing opposite walls so we wouldn’t watch each other, and we were happy in a way I have spent a great deal of money and nearly my life trying to get back to, which is the whole story really, the whole thing in one sentence, so maybe Daniel was right and I should throw out the rest and keep that.

His first book came out when he was twenty-nine. Mine came out eight months later. They were small books from a small press, and they got the kind of reviews that are worse than being ignored, because they used the word promising, which in this business is what they carve on the headstone. A promising debut. We framed the worst sentence from each review and hung them over the table, his and mine, side by side, and we toasted them with the cheap wine, and we meant it, we were not being ironic, we were twenty-nine and thirty and someone had printed our books and put our names on the spines and shelved them in stores where strangers could find them, and we had each other, and we thought the hard part was behind us.

We had our rules by then — not the spoken kind, the other kind, the small private laws two people make without noticing that turn out to be the real constitution of a marriage. We wrote facing opposite walls and never showed each other a word until it was finished, because we’d learned early that a half-made thing shown too soon dies of being looked at. We broke every day at one o’clock, wherever we were and whatever was happening, and that hour was the hinge the whole day turned on. And every night, the last thing before sleep, we read each other the single worst sentence we had written that day — not the best, the worst, the most embarrassing, the one that proved we were frauds — and we laughed at it, and the laughing was what let us go back to the desk in the morning. I have thought about that one a great deal since. We built our whole life on showing each other the worst of ourselves in the dark and laughing, so that neither of us ever had to be alone with it. It turned out to be the only thing we really knew how to do. It turned out to be the only thing that mattered. And it was the one thing we forgot exactly once, at the very end, and the once was enough.

We had one real fight in all those early years, and I’ll tell it to you, because a marriage that never shows you its one real fight is lying to you about something. It was the reviews — the same critic, in the same column, a fortnight apart, called my little book promising and called Daniel’s a disappointment, in that lazy practiced cruelty they use, and I watched it go into him like a splinter too deep to find and pull. And then he did the one thing of his I was never quite able to forgive, which was that he went away. Not out of the apartment. Inside himself. He closed a door I hadn’t known was there and grieved it alone, for a week, courteous and absent, and every night I lay down beside a man who had gone somewhere I wasn’t allowed, and it frightened me more than the review and more than the money, because I had married him precisely so as never to be alone again, and here I was, alone, in a bed with him in it. On the seventh night I couldn’t bear it and I said the thing — I said, you can have the bad review, you can have every bit of it, but you do not get to go in there without me; wherever you go, you take me, the bad places most of all, that is the whole entire point of me. And he looked at me a long time, and something came back into his face that had been gone a week, and he said, you’re right. That’s the deal. I forgot the deal. And we never forgot it again — not once, in all the years, until the very last night of his life. I was twenty-nine. I did not know I had just spoken the one law that would save us over and over, and that would, the single time it was broken, be the end of everything. You never do know which of the things you say in a cheap apartment is the one your whole life will turn on. You just say them, and some of them turn out to be load-bearing, and you find out which ones at the end.

I want to stop here for a second, in the apartment over the dry cleaner, because I was happy there and I didn’t know it, and that is the one unforgivable thing about being young, that the happiness is wasted on you, it runs through your hands like water and you are already looking past it at the next thing, the bigger book, the real reviews, the life that is about to start. I would give anything I have left to stand in that steam-smelling room one more time with the worst sentences of our lives framed on the wall and Daniel facing his wall and me facing mine and the two typewriters going like a pair of slow hearts. I did not know it was the good part. I thought it was the waiting room for the good part.
The good part was already happening. It is always already happening. That is the thing nobody can tell you so that you’ll believe it.
The second books would not come, for either of us, in the city.

I don’t fully understand even now what happened. We had done the thing — we had written the first ones, the hungry ones, the ones you write not knowing if anyone will ever read them, which it turns out is the only way the hungry books get written, in that particular innocence that you only have once. And then people had read them, a few people, enough to print a second, and some part of the machinery that had run so sweetly in the dark seized up the moment a light was on it. I would sit down to write and instead of the story I would hear the reviews. Daniel would sit down and instead of the story he would hear the next review, the one that hadn’t been written yet, the one that was going to decide whether he was a writer or a man who had once written a book. The blank page, which had been a field we ran into, became a wall we sat in front of.

And we had no money. That is the unromantic engine under the whole thing, and I’m going to be honest about it because money is what actually moves people’s lives and novels pretend it isn’t. The city had gotten expensive in the way cities do, quietly and then all at once, and the day jobs ate the hours the books needed, and we were forty-seven and forty-eight years old and we did the arithmetic one night at the same small table, facing each other now because we had long since stopped being shy, and the arithmetic said we could not keep doing this here.

Daniel found Alder. He found it the way he found everything, sideways, following a thread nobody else would have pulled. He was reading about the coal towns, for a book he never wrote, one of the forty books he never wrote, and he came across a photograph of a main street in West Virginia, a real main street, brick, with a river at the end of it and mountains standing up behind the river so steep and so green they looked fake, like a backdrop somebody had hung. And under the photograph it said that you could buy a house there, a whole house, a tall narrow Victorian with a turret and a wraparound porch and colored glass in the front door, for less than one year of our rent.

“Look at this,” he said, and turned the laptop around, and I looked at it, and here is the thing I need you to understand, because everyone afterward wanted it to have been desperation, or foolishness, or running away. It wasn’t. It was hope. We looked at that photograph and we felt hope, pure and specific, the last fully clean hope I think I ever had. A town at the end of the world, cheap and beautiful and forgotten, where nobody knew us and nobody was waiting for our second books, where we could be hungry again on purpose, where the only two typewriters for fifty miles would be ours.

We drove down in October. I will not get the leaves right, so I won’t try; Daniel got the leaves right, once, in the green notebook, and I’ll let him do it. We came over the last ridge and down into the valley and the town was there along the river exactly like the photograph, brick and quiet, the mountains close and enormous, the light coming down gold and sideways through the gaps the way it does in those hollows, and I rolled the window down and the air came in cold and smelling of woodsmoke and the river and something sweet underneath, rotting leaves, the whole mountain breathing out, and I said the thing. There. That one. That’s where the good part starts.
I want that on the record before anything else is. That I said it, and that I was happy, and that I was not wrong.
Here is Daniel, then. The blue notebook, the first week in the house, before the furniture came, when we were sleeping on an air mattress in the turret room because it had the best window.

The house is held up by paint and spite and we love it beyond reason. Clare has claimed the front parlor for her desk because of the colored glass — at four in the afternoon the light comes through the red pane and lies across the floorboards like something spilled, and she says she can’t write without it now, after one day, which is Clare entirely: she finds the one beautiful thing in a room and then cannot live without it, and I married her for this and it will probably bankrupt me.

I have the back room that looks up the mountain. There is a seam of cold that comes under the door at night that no one can find the source of. I have decided it is the previous owner, a Mr. Hollis, dead nineteen years, who dug coal for forty of them and does not approve of two people from the city who have never done a day’s real work buying his house to make up sentences in. I have started saying good morning to the cold seam. Clare thinks this is a bit. It is not a bit. A writer should be on speaking terms with the dead; they are most of the audience.

The town is the most beautiful ruined thing I have ever seen. They took the coal out of these mountains for a hundred years and then one day it was gone or it was cheaper somewhere else, and the companies folded their tents and left, and what they left behind is this — a brick main street built for ten thousand people, with maybe eight hundred left in it, so that the town wears its own grandeur like a good coat three sizes too big on a thin man. The opera house is a furniture store. The furniture store is empty. The bank is a church now and the church is for sale. Everything here used to be something else, and everyone here remembers when, and there is a sadness in that so thick and so gentle that I could write in it forever. I think I could write the real book here. I think we both could. I have not felt this in six years. I had forgotten the feeling had a name.

There is one thing. We went to the pharmacy on the second day, for aspirin and a mousetrap, and there was a line, a real line, a dozen people deep at eleven in the morning, quiet and patient and not quite looking at each other, and I made some joke to the woman ahead of us about small-town rush hour and she looked at me the way you look at a tourist, which is what I was, and said, “You’re not from here,” not unkindly, just placing me, and turned back around. I didn’t understand the line. I understand it now, writing it down, the way you understand things an hour late at the desk, which is the only place I ever understand anything. But that first week I just thought: how strange, how patient, what a lot of sick people for such a small town. And then I forgot about it, because the light was coming through Clare’s red pane, and I had a book in me again, and I was happy.

We were happy for almost two years, and I am not going to rush past them to get to the part everyone’s waiting for, because those two years were real and they were ours and nobody can have them back from us, not the reviewers and not the doctors and not the ones who came to the funeral and held my hands in both of theirs and looked at me as if I were the lesson at the end of a story.

We fixed the house with our own hands, badly. We learned the town. We learned that if you stand still in a place like Alder long enough it stops performing its sadness for you and just lets you in, and underneath the ruin there was a living town, stubborn and funny and kind in the flinty way of people who have been left behind by history and have decided to be decent to each other anyway because there’s no one else coming. We had people to dinner. Daniel grew tomatoes in the side yard and lost a war to the deer about it that gave him more pleasure than winning would have. I started a book, a real one, I could feel it was real, the way you can feel a fever before the thermometer agrees — the second book, the one that would not come in the city, came in Alder, it started to come, slow and strange and mine.

And Daniel’s came too. We wrote in the mornings, facing our separate walls in our separate rooms with the whole breathing mountain around us, and we met in the kitchen at one o’clock the way we always had, and we did not show each other the pages, that was our oldest rule, you do not show until it’s done, but we could tell. You can tell when the person you love is writing well. They carry it differently. They come to lunch already somewhere else. Daniel came to lunch somewhere else for a year and a half and I was so happy for him I could have cried, and sometimes did, in the parlor, in the red light, for no reason I could have told you except that we had bet everything we had on a photograph of a street and it was working.

The blank page was still a wall some mornings. It is always a wall some mornings; that never goes away, and anyone who tells you it does is selling something. But we had learned, over more than twenty years, how to sit in front of the wall and wait, and mostly the waiting worked, and on the mornings it didn’t we would walk down to the river and throw rocks at the water and talk about other people’s books, which is what writers do instead of therapy, and come back and the wall would have a door in it again.

That was the thing we were good at, in the end. Not the writing, though we were all right at the writing. The waiting. We were good at the waiting, together, which is the whole marriage if you boil it down, two people good at waiting in the same room.

I’ll give you one night of it, because the good years were made of nights like it, and I want you to have one to hold the way I hold it. The first winter, a hard one, the kind the mountains do without apology, and the power went out — it went out often in Alder, the lines were old and the company that should have kept them had gone the way of the coal — and the house went dark and cold all at once, the furnace dead, the only light the blue of the snow in the windows. So we did what you do. We carried every candle and every blanket into the parlor with the colored glass, and we built a fire in the fireplace old Mr. Hollis had surely laid a thousand times, and we got down under the blankets together on the floor in front of it, and the snow came past the colored glass, red and gold and blue, and the fire took the cold out of the room an inch at a time. And Daniel read to me — not his own, he never read me his own until it was done, but somebody else’s, a book he loved, in that voice that could make a grocery list sound like scripture — and I lay with my head on his chest and felt each sentence come up through him a half-second before it reached the air, and outside the whole dead beautiful town went white and silent under the snow. And I remember thinking, with my whole body and no words attached to it: this. If it is never once better than this, it has already been enough. I was right. It had already been enough. I had him, and the fire, and the colored snow, and his voice coming up through his chest, and — this is the part that almost never happens to anyone — I knew that I had it while I had it. The happiness did not run through my hands that night. I held it. I am holding it still. It is the one they cannot take, and I have checked, I have checked a thousand times, and it is still here.

I keep circling it. You’ve noticed. I’m an old woman and I’ve told this story to myself ten thousand times and I still circle it, the way you circle a cold lake in summer, knowing you’re going to get in, putting it off, because the first shock of the water is the end of being dry and you want to be dry a little longer.

So let me stay dry one more sentence. It was good. For two years it was so good that I have spent the nine years since both grateful and ruined for having had it, because now I know what the top of my own life looked like and I was standing on it and I did not feel the air thinning.
The accident was in March. Daniel was driving.

That is where the good years end, and I find I cannot write past the sentence tonight, so I won’t. He got the leaves right, up above, so I’ll stop on his page and not mine. Tomorrow I’ll tell you about the road, and the hospital in the next county, and the kind young doctor, and the little amber bottle they sent us home with, that we were so grateful for, that we set on the kitchen windowsill in the sun like it was nothing, like it was aspirin, like it was the most ordinary thing in the world.
It was the most ordinary thing in the world. That was what none of us knew yet. That it comes into the house looking exactly like mercy.
II. MERCY

The day it happened was one of the good ones. I need you to know that first, before the road and the tree, because the people who come to a story like this one always arrange the light backward, so that the whole last good day is lit from underneath by what’s coming, every ordinary thing already a little bit doomed. It wasn’t like that. We didn’t have that light. We had the real light, the kind you can’t see by, and in the real light it was simply a good day, maybe the best one we’d had in Alder, and I would not give it back even now, even knowing it was the last of its kind.

It was the end of March, a Thursday, nearly two years after we’d come over the ridge with the windows down. The winter had been long the way mountain winters are, not dramatic, just gray and patient and endless, the river running black between white banks, and that Thursday the first real warmth came up the valley and the ice let go of the eaves all morning with a sound like someone setting down glasses in another room. And Daniel had gotten a letter. A real letter, on real paper, from an editor in New York who had read his first book years ago and never forgotten it, asking — not promising, asking — to see the new one when it was ready. After six years of silence. He read it to me in the kitchen three times and then he said, “Put your good dress on, Clare, we’re driving to Beckett’s.”

Beckett’s was the one restaurant in the county seat, forty minutes over the mountain, where the tablecloths were cloth and they knew how to cook a trout, and we had been there exactly twice, both times for something that mattered. So I put my good dress on, the dark green one, and Daniel wore the jacket that still fit him in the shoulders, and we drove over the mountain in the long gold light of the first warm evening of the year, and we were happy. I want to spend one more sentence inside that car while it’s still whole. The windows were cracked because the warmth was real and we wanted it, and the river ran beside us down in its gorge throwing back the last of the sun, and Daniel drove with one hand and held mine on the console with the other, and we talked about the book, his book, the one the letter wanted, and whether he’d send it in the fall, and what we’d do if — and we let the if hang there, the good if, the one we hadn’t let ourselves say out loud in years. That is the last thing. The two of us in the green dress and the good jacket with a good if hanging in the warm air of the car, driving over a mountain to celebrate a letter.

We had the trout. We had a bottle of wine, one bottle, between us, over two hours, I have done that arithmetic too and it is not the answer, the wine is not the answer, I had two glasses and Daniel had two and a half and we drove home sober under a sky gone from gold to green to the deep used blue of a spring night in the mountains. It had started to rain by the time we left Beckett’s, a fine cold rain, the kind that can’t decide if it’s sleet, and the road home climbs out of the county seat and runs the ridge for a few miles before it drops back down to Alder along the river, and it was up on the ridge, in the dark, in the rain that couldn’t decide, coming around the long slow bend by the old church camp, that the deer stepped out.

I have thought about the deer more than I have thought about almost anything. It was a doe. She came out of the dark on the left and she did not run; that is the thing people get wrong; a deer in your headlights does not run, she stops, she turns her whole head and looks at you, and for a quarter of a second you and the deer are the only two living things on earth and you are both completely certain the other one is about to do something and neither of you does. Daniel did what your hands do before your mind is consulted. He turned the wheel away from her, to the right, hard, and the back of the car came loose on the wet road the way a thing comes loose that has been waiting all its life to come loose, and we left the road.

It was not fast. I will say it again because it is the truest and least believable thing: it was not fast. We slid off the right shoulder and down a short grassy slope, and there was a moment, a long impossible moment, where it was almost gentle, where we were just two people in a car going somewhere soft and sideways in the dark, and I had time to say his name, once, calmly, Daniel, the way you’d say it to wake him, and then the slope delivered us to the oak.

The oak had been there two hundred years. It took the front of the car on my side and it did not move an inch and it did not care. There was the one enormous flat sound, the sky’s door slamming, and the window blew into glitter, and the whole front of the car on my side came inward to meet me — the dash, the floor, the place where my legs had been — folded back like the lid of something, and then the rain, suddenly, everywhere, loud on what was left of the roof, and the horn going in one long idiot note, and Daniel’s voice, Daniel’s voice saying my name over and over, Clare, Clare, Clare, and me not answering, not because I couldn’t hear him but because all of my attention, every part of me, had gone down to my left leg, which was somewhere it should not be, under what used to be the dashboard, and was sending up the first word of a message my body would spend the next year receiving.

We were up on that ridge in the rain for fifty-one minutes before anyone came. I know it was fifty-one minutes because Daniel, who could not turn his body, could move his left hand, and he found his phone in the door pocket, and he called, and the dispatcher stayed on with him, and afterward they told us the time of the call and the time the truck reached us, and I have kept those two numbers the way you keep things that have no use.

Alder has a volunteer fire company and a single ambulance that lives behind the old hardware store, and the men who drive it have day jobs, and they came as fast as men can come who have to first leave their suppers and their couches and drive to the station in the rain. Fifty-one minutes. In the city an ambulance is a sound you resent, a thing that wakes you. Out here it is a prayer with a long way to travel.

So we waited, and I am going to tell you about the waiting, because it was the first of the things we shared that no one outside will ever credit as anything but horror, and it was horror, and it was also ours, and I have never been able to lay it down. Daniel could not reach me with his body — his chest was wrong, every breath was a knife, I could hear it in him, a wet catch at the top of each one — but he could reach my hand, and he did, across the broken console, through the cold rain coming in where the roof had opened, and he held it, and he talked to me. He did not tell me it would be all right. That is one of the ten thousand things I loved him for and did not know to count until later: in the worst moment of our lives he did not insult me with it’s going to be all right. He talked to me about the book. He talked to me, in the dark, in the rain, with his ribs broken and my leg crushed and the horn finally dying into silence and the cold coming up through everything, about the ending of the novel the letter wanted, which he had not figured out, and he figured it out aloud, to keep me with him, to keep us both on this side of the dark, and I held his hand and I listened and I put in a word here and there when I could find the breath, and somewhere up the slope, at the top, where the headlights still pointed uselessly into the rain, the doe came back. I saw her. She stood at the top of the slope and looked down at what we had done to keep from touching her, and then she turned, unhurried, and was gone, and I did not hate her and I do not hate her now. She was doing what she was for. We were all just doing what we were for, out there in the rain, waiting for the men to leave their suppers.
They took me away from him first, and that was the second thing, the splitting, and it frightened me more than the pain.

My leg was what they call an open break — the bone had come through — and the big hospital that could fix it was more than an hour away by road, too far, so they sent the helicopter. I had never been in a helicopter. I want to tell you I remember the flight, the lights of the valley, something beautiful to put there, but the truth is they had given me something by then, into the back of my hand, the first of the medicine, the very first, and the flight is gone, and the next thing I have is white light and a voice asking me my name and the strange fact that I could not feel the leg that an hour before had been the entire world. That was the medicine. The first mercy. It did not fix anything. It stood between me and the thing, the way, I would learn, it always does, and in that first hour it was the kindest thing that had ever happened to me, and I have to hold that memory and the nine years that followed in the same two hands and not drop either, which is the work, which is the whole of the work.

Daniel came the long way, by road, by ambulance, an hour behind me, and so for the worst night of our lives we were in two different buildings in two different counties, each not knowing if the other was alive, and I have come to think that the drug knew its business from that first night: it had already begun to teach us that the unbearable thing is to be apart in it, and the bearable thing, the almost sweet thing, is to be in it together.

I will tell you what they did to us, plainly, because you should know what the body pays, and because the people who tell these stories usually skip from the crash to the needle as if the year between them were an intermission, and that year was not an intermission, that year was where it happened, in the slow daylight, with everyone being kind.

My leg they first held together from the outside, with a frame of metal rods standing off the skin and steel pins running down through the flesh into the bone, to keep the broken pieces still until the swelling went down. Then, a week later, a surgeon I would never meet opened the leg along its length and laid a steel rod down the hollow center of the big bone and closed it over, and fixed the cracked ring of my pelvis with a flat plate and a row of screws, and that is the metal I still carry, that still wakes in the cold, that the airport machines still find. They told me not to put any weight on that side for ten weeks. Ten weeks. A body is not built to be told that. You do not know, until you are told you may not stand on your own leg, how much of being a person is simply standing on your own legs.

Daniel they could do less for, which was somehow worse. You cannot cast a rib. His three broken ribs they could only wrap and wait on, and the waiting was dangerous — a person whose every breath hurts begins, without meaning to, to breathe shallow, and the bottom of the lungs goes still and wet, and that is how the quiet pneumonias start that kill people the crash didn’t. So they gave him a small plastic thing to breathe into, with a float you had to lift with your own breath, ten times an hour, all day, each breath a knife, to keep himself alive by hurting himself on purpose, and I will never forget the sound of it from the next bed once they finally put us in the same room, the slow suck and the little rattle of the float, my husband hurting himself ten times an hour to stay. His right wrist, the writing wrist, they fixed with a small plate and two pins and a cast. And his back — the deep injury, the one that mattered — one of the soft cushions between the bones of his spine had been shoved out of place in the crash and was pressing on the big nerve that runs down into the leg, and that one they could not cut out and could not set and could not wrap. That one, they said, might settle on its own with time. It never did. That was the one that never let him go, the low constant speaking of it, the thing that meant that for the rest of his life there would always be a reason, a real reason, an honest reason, to reach for the amber bottle. The crash gave him a pain with no end, and then the world gave him the thing that ends pain, and told him it was medicine, and it was medicine, and that is not a trick anyone played on us. That is just how it goes. That is the thing itself.
They brought us home in May, to a house we could not climb.

The turret room with the best window was two flights up and might as well have been on the moon. So we lived in the front parlor, the one with the colored glass, that whole spring and summer — they wheeled in two narrow rented beds and set them side by side where the dining table had been, and that is where we were, the two of us, in the red and gold light that came through the glass in the late afternoon and lay across the floor like something spilled, which Daniel had loved on the first day and which we now watched travel across the boards for hours because there was very little else we could do.

I am going to tell you about those months the way they were, which is not the way Ruth tells them. Ruth — Daniel’s younger sister, who drove down from Ohio when she heard and stayed six weeks and was, I want to say clearly, magnificent, who cooked and cleaned and drove us the hour to our appointments and emptied the things that have to be emptied when two people cannot walk — Ruth remembers those months as the beginning of the horror, the first chapter of the thing that took her brother. And she is not wrong. The horror did begin there. But that is not what those months were, from inside them, and I am the only one left who was inside them, so I get to say.

They were, God help me, tender. They were among the most tender months of our marriage. There is an intimacy in being broken together that I had no idea existed, that I would not have traded, that I am not sure I would trade now. We had been married nearly thirty years and I thought I knew what it was to be close to a person, and then I learned what it is to help that person do the things a body does not let another person help with, the small humiliating mechanical things, and to have them help you, and to find that there is no humiliation in it at all once you are both far enough down, that it burns off, that what’s left when the dignity goes is something better than dignity, something I don’t have a good word for even now. We learned each other’s bodies the way you learn a language by living where it’s spoken. Daniel could not raise his arms, so I washed his hair in a basin, leaning out of my bed into his, both of us swearing and laughing, the water going everywhere. I could not get to the bathroom alone for a long time, and he was the one — ribs and all, hurting himself worse to do it — who got me there, who would not let the visiting nurse do it when he could, because, he said, he was not going to miss the chance to carry me over a threshold again, and he said it as a joke, and it was not a joke, and we both knew it wasn’t, and that is the whole of what I mean by the thing I don’t have a word for.

And every morning and every evening, there were the amber bottles, lined up now on the mantel over the cold fireplace, his and mine, with the typed labels and the cotton in the top and our own names, and we took what they told us to take, because we hurt, because the man they sent us to, Dr. Prewitt, the one doctor in Alder, told us to, and he was kind, and he was tired, and he had a waiting room full of broken mountain people and forty years of watching them hurt, and he gave us what the hospital had started and what our broken bodies plainly needed, and not one person in this part of the story did a single thing wrong. That is what I most need you to understand before we go on. Everyone was kind. Everyone did the sensible, merciful, correct thing at every step. The nurse was kind and the surgeon was kind and Dr. Prewitt was kind and Ruth was magnificent and Daniel and I loved each other more in that parlor than we ever had in our lives, and all of it, every kindness, every correct and merciful step, was carrying us deeper into the country we would not find our way back out of together. There was no villain. I have looked. For nine years I have looked for the villain and there isn’t one, and that is the worst thing I know about the world, worse than if there were.

Here is Daniel, from the green notebook, a June night in the parlor, the casts off by then but the pain of the back fully moved in, his handwriting its own right-handed self again, going a little downhill toward the gutter.

Everyone has left for the night. Ruth has gone back to Ohio, having saved our lives and refused all thanks. The nurse comes only twice a week now. It is just us again, Clare asleep in the next bed three feet away, and the red light gone from the glass hours ago, and the mountain out there in the dark being patient the way it is always being patient.

The back is bad tonight. I won’t describe it; I’ve been describing it for weeks and the describing has started to bore even me, which is a mercy of its own. I waited as long as I could and then I took what Prewitt gives me, and I have been lying here in the dark waiting for it, and about twenty minutes ago it came, and I have to write this down while it’s clean, because I think it is the most important thing that has happened to me since the oak tree, and because I have noticed that I am already a little bit afraid of it, and a man should write down the thing he is afraid of while he can still see it plainly.

It is not that the pain stops. I have said this before and got it slightly wrong, so let me get it right tonight. The pain does not stop. What stops is the pain’s dominion. For weeks the pain has been the government of my body — it has set every policy, it decides when I move and how I breathe and whether I can bear to be spoken to — and twenty minutes ago, quietly, without a shot fired, the government fell. The pain is still down there. I can see it, a small deposed thing in the corner, muttering. But it governs nothing now. And into the enormous space where its government used to be, everything else comes flooding — the whole world I’d forgotten was out there past the dirty window of it.

And here is what I did not expect and what I am afraid of. It is not just the pain’s government that falls. It is all of them. The whole committee that runs a man — the one that keeps the accounts, the one that remembers the bad reviews, the one that stands behind my right shoulder at the desk and tells me I am a fraud, the one that has been afraid, quietly, of one thing or another, every single day since I was a boy and did not even know fear had a sound until tonight, when it stopped. They all fall. And what is left, when the whole anxious government of a man is deposed, is a thing I can only call peace, and I am fifty years old and I am ashamed to tell even this notebook that I do not think I have ever felt it before, not once, not on my wedding day, not holding my first book, not any of the days I would have told you were the happy ones. This is the happy one. This quiet. This nothing-wrong. This room with Clare breathing in it and the mountain out there and no government at all.

It is like the moment in deep snow when you stop walking and the whole forest stops with you and you understand that silence is not the absence of sound but a thing in itself, with mass, that you could lean against. It is like the first second after you finally set down a weight you’d been carrying so long you’d forgotten it was a weight and had started to think the ache was just the shape of your own shoulders. It is like — and I’ll write this one and then put down the pen and let myself have the rest of it — it is like being held. Just that. Like being held by something that asks nothing and wants nothing and is not even particularly interested in you, that simply holds you the way the dark holds the mountain, and lets you, for an hour, not have to be the one doing the carrying.

Clare takes hers too. We don’t talk about it much. We take them at the same time, most nights, without planning to, and we lie here three feet apart in the two little beds in the dark, and I know — I can hear it in how her breathing changes — I know when hers arrives, and she knows when mine does, and we reach across the gap between the beds and hold hands, and we are, for that hour, in the same held place at the same time, two people in the one warmth, and I will tell you the truth because this notebook is the only thing I don’t lie to: it is the closest I have ever felt to another human being, and the other human being is my wife of nearly thirty years, and we got there by driving into a tree. I don’t know what to do with that. I don’t think there is anything to do with it except write it down, and take her hand, which I am going to do now, because I can hear that hers has just come.

So that is where I’ll leave us tonight, the way I left us at the end of the first part — on his page and not mine, because he was always better, and because I cannot improve on it and would not try. Two people three feet apart in the dark, holding hands across the gap, in the one warmth, at the top of the second good season of our lives.

We did not know it was a door. We thought it was a room. We thought we had been let, at last, after the oak tree and the metal and the long humbling spring, into a small warm room where nothing hurt and nothing was wrong, and we thought we could come and go from it as we pleased, the way you come and go from a room.

I know what it was now. I have learned its name and its history and what it does to the lock it fits, and I’ll tell you all of it, because Daniel would want you to have the real thing under the made-up thing. But I wanted you to feel it first the way we felt it, with no name on it, because if you do not understand that it was the most beautiful room we ever entered, you will not understand anything about why we could not leave it, and you will do what Ruth does, what the world does, what the people at the funeral did with their two hands around mine — you will call it a tragedy and feel sorry for us, and we did not want, either of us, not then and not at the end, to be felt sorry for. We wanted to be understood. That is why I am writing this. That is the only reason.
III. THE GOD WHO WEARS YOUR FACE
It was Daniel who gave it its true name, that summer, over lunch, the way we had handed each other everything interesting for nearly thirty years.

By then we were up on our feet again, more or less. I was on a cane and would be for the rest of my life; the metal in my leg had knit the bone back into something that worked and would never again be innocent. Daniel’s ribs had healed and his wrist had healed and only the deep thing in his back was left, the one that had moved in to stay, so that he stood and sat and turned over in the night the careful way of a man who shares his body with a sleeping dog he mustn’t wake. We had moved back upstairs. We were writing again — I’ll get to how we were writing. And the amber bottles had moved with us, from the parlor mantel to the kitchen windowsill to the drawer in the hall, Dr. Prewitt refilling them each month without my ever quite having to ask, because the back was real and the leg was real and the pain was, I want to keep saying this, real.

Daniel read the way other people breathe, and one afternoon he came to the kitchen at one o’clock already somewhere else, which I had learned years ago to love as the sign that the work was running, and he set down a cold sandwich he wasn’t going to eat and said, “Did you know they named it after a god?”
I said named what.

“What we take. The grandmother of it, anyway.” And he told me, and I’m going to give it to you the way he gave it to me, because Daniel always wanted the reader to have the real thing under the made-up thing, and because this was the moment the lovely nameless warmth we had been living inside got its name, and a thing with a name is a different thing to live with than a thing without one.

The medicine in our bottles, he said, was a great-grandchild of a single plant. A poppy — the tall kind with the fat green seed-head that bleeds a white milk when you score it. People had known for thousands of years that the dried milk of that one poppy took away pain, and fear, and grief, and gave you, in their place, a warm half-sleep full of good dreams. And a little over two hundred years ago, a young man in Germany, a pharmacist’s apprentice barely out of his teens, had done something nobody had managed before: he had pulled the one pure powerful thing out of all that poppy milk, the white powder at the very heart of the white milk, the thing that did the work. And he had to name it. And he was young, and it was that kind of century, full of poets, so he reached for the oldest story he knew and named his white powder after a god — not a big god, a quiet one, the Greek god of dreams, the one who slips into a sleeper’s room at night and stands by the bed wearing the face of someone the sleeper loves, so that the dead come back in dreams, and the far-away come close, and no one wakes alone.

“He named it after the god,” Daniel said, turning the cold sandwich in his good hand, lit up, delighted, “who comes to you in the night wearing the face of someone you love. Clare. Isn’t that exactly it. Isn’t that precisely and completely what it does.”

I laughed. God help me, I laughed, because it was exactly it, and because noticing exactly-it across a lunch table was the whole reason we had moved to the end of the world, and I thought: there he is, there’s my husband, lit from inside, finding the true lovely thing in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday. I did not hear the eulogy inside the marvel. He was telling me the name of the thing that was going to kill him and he was telling it as a wonder, the god who wears the face of someone you love, and he was right, that is exactly what it does, that is exactly and precisely and finally what it does — it comes to you wearing the face of everything you love, your work and your wife and the end of your pain, all at once, so that to push it away you would have to push away everything whose face it wears.

That was the last fully happy conversation I can set a date to. I have gone back to it ten thousand times. I would live in it if I could, the kitchen, the mountain in the window, the cold sandwich, my husband delighted by a dead god’s name, neither of us hearing the door quietly open behind the word.

Now I’ll tell you how we were writing, because if I don’t make you believe this part, the rest is just a sad story about weak people, and it was not that, and I did not spend nine years and a marriage learning what it was in order to let you think it was that.
We were writing the best work of our lives.

I can prove it, which is the terrible part. I have the pages. I have read them stone-sober nine years later with the cruelest eye I own, looking for the lie, wanting to find that the warmth had fooled us, that the great stuff was really garbage we’d been too far gone to see — because that would be easier, that would let me file those months under delusion and close the drawer. But it isn’t true. Some of what we wrote that summer and that autumn is the best either of us ever did. I know good writing; it’s the one thing I have never been able to lie to myself about; and it was good.

Here is what the warmth did, and why it is the most dangerous thing I have ever known, more dangerous than the oak tree, because the oak tree only took our bodies. You know the one who stands behind your right shoulder at the desk, whose entire job is to tell you it isn’t good enough, it’s been done before, you’re a fraud, the sentence you just wrote is the one that will finally prove it? Every writer has him. Most people have some version of him at whatever they’re trying to do. The warmth sent him out of the room. It didn’t argue with him. It just closed the door behind him, gently, the way you close a door on a sleeping child, and for the first time in six years I was alone with the page the way I’d been alone with it at twenty-four, before I knew enough to be afraid.

The words came. For both of us, in our separate rooms, all through that long green summer and into the gold of the fall. We met at one o’clock and we broke the oldest rule we had, the one about not showing until it’s done, and we read each other pages in the afternoon light, and the pages were good, and we knew they were good, and we were — I am not going to soften this, I have softened everything else — we were happy. We were two real writers having the best season of our lives, and we were having it because every morning we were a little bit not in our right minds, and both of those facts are true at once, and holding them both at once without dropping either is the whole reason this book exists.

I’ll give you one afternoon of it, one real one, because the season was made of afternoons like it, and because I have it still and I want you to have it too. It was late August, the heat finally letting go, and Daniel came into the kitchen at one o’clock not with a cold sandwich this time but with three pages in his hand, and I knew before he said a word, by the way he was carrying his own body — lightly, the way you carry it when you’ve just set something heavy down. “Read this,” he said. “I’ve lost the place you see it from.” Which was a lie; he could always tell; but he wanted to give it to me, and I had been wanting for a week to give him mine. So we broke the oldest rule we had, the one about not showing a word until it’s done, the way we broke everything, together.

The pages were about the town. About an old miner who had gone down into the mountain forty winters and been let go at the end of it into a place that no longer needed the thing he had spent his body to bring up.

He stood on Main Street in the long gold evening with the opera house behind him gone to selling other men’s furniture, and he understood, the way you understand a death, that the town had only ever been a coat the coal wore — and the coal was gone, and the coat did not know yet that it was empty, and went on standing in the cold in the shape of a man.

I set the pages down and I could not speak, and that was the review, the only one that ever counted for either of us: the silence of the other one with your pages in their lap. He had never written anything that good in his life. I told him so, and then I got my own, the ones I had been afraid of, and he read them at the same table in the same red light and set them down and looked at me and said nothing, and the nothing was the whole of it. Two people at the top of the one thing they had given their lives to, in a kitchen at the end of the world, the mountain in the window, the work coming in through a door that the fear had kept shut for years and that now stood open.

And it came through that door. Not past it — through it. The best work either of us ever did came through the same door, in the same warmth, that was already, that same gold afternoon, quietly killing us. I have the pages; they are in the drawer three feet from where I am writing this; they are exactly as good as I remember, I have checked, and every time I check I have to take the two things up in my two hands again and not drop either: that it was the warmth that held the door open, and that it was the warmth that was going to close it, on all of it, for good. You cannot take the one without the other. That is the thing the people outside cannot hold, and it is the whole of what I know.

Ruth calls those months the honeymoon. The counselors taught her the word; it’s the pretty name they use for the lie at the beginning, the bait on the hook. And I understand why she needs it to have been a lie, because if it was only a lie then her brother was only a victim, and a victim is a clean thing to grieve. But I was inside it, and I am telling you from inside it, across nine years and his death: it was not only a lie. It was also the truest work and the closest we ever were. And the thing I cannot forgive, the thing I have written a whole book trying to lay my hand on, is that there was no seam. The lie and the truth came through the same door, in the same warmth, wearing the same beloved face. You could not take the one without the other. Nobody can. That is not weakness. That is the design.
The first crack was so small that I only know it was the first because I have had nine years to lay them all in a row and look for where the line begins.

It was the autumn. I was at my desk in the morning, in the red light through the glass, and I reached for the warmth the way I had every morning for months, to send the man behind my shoulder out of the room so I could work — and it worked, but not all the way. He went, but he stood just outside the door now, and I could feel him there, and the words came but they came against a faint resistance, as if through one thin layer of something, and I did the most natural thing in the world, the thing anyone would do, the thing the whole trap is built to make you do: I decided I needed a little more. Not a lot. A little. Because the back pain was worse, I told myself, and it may even have been true, who can ever untangle it, that is the genius of it again — and I took a little more, and the man went all the way out, and I worked, and I thought nothing of it.

I want to tell you what was actually happening, because Daniel figured it out that same autumn, from a book, the way he figured out everything, and brought it to me at lunch not delighted this time but quiet, turning it over.

The warmth was never a gift the drug added to us. It was a door the body already had. Every one of us is born with our own private supply of something very like it — the body makes its own, in small amounts, and releases it in trickles: the calm after you’ve been hurt and the hurt starts to ebb, the warmth of being held, the second wind, the quiet after weeping. We have our own, and it is metered out, a drop at a time, exactly as much as a life can bear. What we had been pouring into ourselves every morning was a flood where the body deals in drops — the same key, the same lock, turned a thousand times harder than the body ever turns it.

And the body is not a fool. The body, finding its own lock being thrown wide open every single day by a flood from outside, does the sensible thing, the thrifty thing, the thing it has done for every creature for a billion years: it turns its own supply down. Why keep making your own warmth, why keep the locks oiled and the drops flowing, when a flood arrives every morning from the kitchen drawer? So it turns itself down. It turns itself down a little more each day. And that is why the same amount that lifted us like angels in the spring did a little less by the autumn, and why I needed a little more to get back to where I’d been — not because I was weak, not because I wanted more pleasure, but because the floor had quietly moved. The body had been turning down its own lights to match the flood, so that now, underneath the flood, the room was darker than it had ever been before any of this began, and the flood was no longer lifting me to heaven. It was lifting me back up to ordinary. And ordinary, now, was only reachable by flood.

That is the whole thing. That is the entire mechanism, and there is nothing else to it, and it is the saddest machine I know of, and we were already deep inside it before Daniel read it out to me at the lunch table, quiet, turning the book over in his hands, the two of us finally beginning, just beginning, to be afraid.
The night I understood we were not going to be able to just stop, I have never told anyone, and I am going to tell you, and then I am going to stop for tonight, because it still costs me.

It was a Sunday, late fall, and we had decided — lightly, the way you decide to skip dessert — that we’d take the day off from it. Just the one day. To prove we could. We didn’t say prove we could; we said something easy, we said let’s give our heads a rest, and we meant it, and we were, I think, still mostly sure it would be nothing.

By the afternoon Daniel was wrong in a way I had no name for. He was restless in his skin. He couldn’t sit in his chair, couldn’t lie down, couldn’t read, which for Daniel was like a fish unable to be in water. He was sweating though the house was cold, and then cold though he was sweating, and his nose ran, and his eyes watered, and he kept yawning these enormous involuntary yawns, and his legs — he kept moving his legs, bending and straightening them, pacing, because, he said, they felt like they wanted to crawl off his body, like there were ants under the bone, and nothing he did made it stop. By evening I wasn’t much better. A low grinding dread had come up in me out of nowhere, worse than any fear I’d ever felt because it had no face, no cause, it was just there, rising, the exact opposite of the warmth, the warmth turned inside out, and every cell I had was leaning toward the drawer in the hall the way a field of flowers leans at the sun.

We lasted until nearly ten o’clock. I remember the clock. And then Daniel stood up in the middle of the cold bright kitchen, grey-faced, shaking, this brilliant funny gentle man I had loved for nearly thirty years, and he looked at me, and I looked at him, and neither of us said the thing out loud because we didn’t have to. We just — both of us, together, without a word, the way we did everything — we went and got the bottles.

And the relief, when it came, twenty minutes later, was not heaven. That’s the part nobody tells you. It wasn’t heaven anymore. It was just the ants stopping. It was just the dread lifting back to ordinary. It was the flood coming in only high enough, now, to reach the place where we could stand being alive, and we sat in the dark kitchen feeling the horror recede, not lifted, not transported, just returned, just allowed back to zero, and we held hands across the table, and we did not talk about the god who wears the face of someone you love, because we had both just met the face he wears when you try to send him away.

That was the autumn the door locked behind us. We didn’t hear it. You never hear it. That is the one thing every single person who has been through that door will tell you, the one thing they all agree on across every country and every century: there is no click. You are in the warm room, free, coming and going as you please, and then one ordinary Sunday you reach for the door to step out for the day, the way you have a hundred times, and it does not open, and it has not opened since, and you cannot for your life remember which of the hundred times before was the last time it did.
THE JOY PLANT

Step out of the story for a moment, and go back. Not years — thousands of years. Past the cars and the hospitals and the little amber bottles, past the cities, past writing itself, to the far edge of what we can still see at all. The people in this part have no books, because books have not been invented. They have just learned to farm. They live in small settlements of mud and reed around the shores of the warm middle sea and the two rivers east of it, and they have begun, for the first time in the whole life of our kind, to put seeds in the ground on purpose and wait. And one of the first things they plant — older than the wheel, older than the letter A — is a poppy.

We have the seeds. That is how we know. In caves and old graves around the Mediterranean, in Spain and Switzerland and Germany, people have dug up the small hard seeds of this one particular poppy, left by people who lived more than seven thousand years ago, before 5000 BC. In one cave in Spain that they call the Bat Cave, the seed-heads were laid among the dead in small baskets woven of grass, on purpose, and you only bury a plant with your dead when the plant is something more than food.

And we know a little of how they grew it, because the poppy is a patient teacher and has not much changed its habits in all the time since. It is not a hard plant to please. It wants only what the first farmers already had to give — turned ground, full sun, a dry season, a temperate sky — and it pays them back out of all proportion: a tall gray-green stalk, a flower of white or lilac or deep red that opens for a day or two and falls, and then, where the flower was, a fat round head the size of a child’s fist, swelling and ripening from green toward the color of straw. On the shores of the Italian lakes, and in the villages built out over the water on wooden posts in what is now Switzerland, farmers seven and eight thousand years ago grew it in their small plots beside their wheat and their barley, and we have found it there by the handful in the lake-mud under the old house-floors — so much of it, so carefully kept, that it was plainly no curiosity but a crop, one of the ordinary things a family grew in order to live. They ate the seeds, which are only food and hold no sleep in them at all. And somewhere in those first farming centuries they learned the other thing the head will give you, if you ask it in the right way.

Nobody wrote down why, because nobody yet could. The first people who could write, the Sumerians, between the two rivers, grew it in their fields more than five thousand years ago, and on their clay tablets — the oldest writing of any kind that we have, the first words our species ever set down — they left a name for it. The name, as far as anyone can read it, was hul gil [hool GEEL]. The joy plant. The people who read that ancient writing for a living still argue over it, and you should know that; but that is the name that has come down to us across five thousand years, from the first hand that ever wrote anything, for this flower: joy. And they wrote down how they took it — scoring the fat green seed-head so the white milk weeps out, and gathering it in the morning, the way you gather anything precious that the night has made.

The way is this, and it has scarcely changed in all the centuries, in any country on earth. You wait until the petals have fallen and the head is full and still green, and in the cool of the evening you take a small blade and score it — a few shallow lines, just through the skin, no deeper — and then you leave it alone overnight. In the dark the wound weeps. By morning the whole head is beaded with a milk gone brown and sticky in the air, and you walk out at first light and gather it, scraping each scored head gentle and clean, and that stooping in the early light from one head to the next is one of the oldest motions our hands still know how to make. Far from those lake-villages, and long after them, on the island of Crete, someone shaped a little clay goddess no taller than your hand and set upon her head a crown of three poppy heads — and carved into the clay of each one a set of shallow cuts, the very slits of the evening scoring, so that across three thousand years and a lost language we can still read what the people who knelt to her knew: this flower, and this small blade, and this gathering in the morning, and that they thought the whole of it holy enough to crown a god with.

After them, everyone. In Egypt they grew whole fields of it in the hot black soil the river laid down each year, and the best of it came from around the southern city of Thebes, and the priests and the healers kept it close; for centuries afterward people still called the finest kind by the name of that one city, the way you might name a wine for its valley. And the Greeks, who gave us so many of our words, gave us this one too: they called the white milk opion [OP-ee-on], which only means the juice — the sap, the thing that weeps out — and that plain little word, worn smooth by three thousand years of mouths, is the one we still say. Opium. It only ever meant the juice.

But the Greeks saw what was under the medicine. They put the poppy into the hands of their gods of sleep, and of night, and of death — the three brothers of oblivion — because they understood that this flower’s true gift was a kind of beautiful forgetting. And in Homer’s old poem, the oldest story we keep, there is a moment at a sad feast where a woman slips a drug into the wine, a drug that takes away grief and the memory of pain, so that a man could sit and hear how his own brother died and not weep. The Greeks called that drug nepenthe [neh-PEN-thee] — it means, simply, no grief — and for three thousand years people have read that line and thought: that was the poppy. We can’t be sure. But we know the poppy can do exactly that. We know, for certain, that it can take away grief.

And that is the oldest thing about it — older than the needle, older than the law, older than the crisis, older than any name on any bottle. For as long as there have been people, there has been this one flower that takes away pain and fear and grief and leaves a warm forgetting where they were, and for as long as there have been people, people have wanted it, and reached for it, and buried it with their dead. Clare and Daniel, in their parlor, three feet apart in the dark, holding hands in the one warmth — they believed they had found a small, private, modern room that the accident had opened for them alone.
They had walked into the oldest room there is.
IV. THE CHEAPER, NEARER THING
The pills went away the way everything goes away now — not with a decision anyone would own, but with a policy.

Somewhere far above Alder, in rooms we never saw, the people who count things had finally begun to count the dead, and the number had gotten big enough to move, and the thing that moved was the supply. They tightened the rules on men like Dr. Prewitt. They put his prescriptions into a state computer that watched him the way nothing had ever watched him in forty years of watching sick people, and they sent him letters, and they made examples of two doctors a county over, and Dr. Prewitt, who was tired, and kind, and near the end of a long life of being the only one, did the only safe thing left to him. He began, gently, to turn us down.

He did it the right way. That is its own small horror. He did not cut us off at the knees; he sat us down, Daniel and me, in his brown office with the diplomas going yellow on the wall, and he told us the truth, which was that the thing in our bottles had stopped being medicine for us somewhere back in the fall and become something else, and that the kindest thing he could do now was to help us down off it slowly, a little less each month, a long gentle staircase back to the ground. He meant it. He was trying to save us. And every word he said was correct, and I sat there nodding, and the entire time he was talking, some newer, colder part of me that I was only just meeting was doing arithmetic, was counting the pills left in the drawer at home against the days, and was already, before I had even left his office, afraid in a way that had nothing to do with anything he was saying.

Because a gentle staircase is a beautiful idea, and the body does not care about beautiful ideas. The body only knows the floor has moved, and that each lower step is a step down into the ants and the dread and the warmth turned inside out, held there on purpose, by design, for a month at a time. We tried the staircase. I want that on the record too: we tried, for a while, to go down it the way he asked. And it was like being asked to lower yourself into cold water an inch a day and stay there. No one can do it. A few people can do it. We were not among them, and I have stopped being ashamed of that, because I have met the few who can, in the years since, in the rooms, and they are not better than we were. They are just people the machine happened to let go of. The machine did not let go of us.

So one grey afternoon in the dead of that second winter, with the staircase shaking under us and the dread coming up, a man we knew a little — a good man, a man whose own brother was in it, half the town was in it, you have to understand that about Alder, this was not a dark corner, this was the whole house — this man told Daniel, kindly, the way you’d tell a neighbor where to get his snow tires cheaper, that there was another way to not be sick. Nearer. Cheaper. It came from the same flower, he said, it did the same thing, it was the same warmth; it had just been carried one more step down the same long road from the field to the street. It had a name we both knew, the way you know the name of a city you have sworn you will never have any reason to visit.

Heroin. There. I have written it. It took me until the fourth part of this book to write it, because it took us until the second winter to say it in our own kitchen, and I wanted you to come to it the way we did — not as the thing this was always going to be about, not as the monster on the poster, but as the cheaper, nearer thing, offered kindly by a decent man on a grey day, that did the same thing the medicine did, that we already could not live without, and that was now the only door left in a room we could not get out of.

I am not going to tell you how. I want to be very clear about that, here, at the worst threshold in this book. There is a way these stories get told where the crossing over becomes a kind of dark recipe, where the reader leans in, and I will not do it, not because I am protecting you but because there is nothing on the other side of that leaning-in that is worth one single thing, and because the how was never the point. The how is the least interesting thing about the worst day of your life. What matters is the line, and that we crossed it, and that we crossed it together.

Because there was a line. We had one. Everyone in it has one, some last thing they swear they will never do, the thing that in their own private ranking is where the real addicts are and they are not, and ours was the obvious one, the one with the needle in it, the one that turns us, two writers who had an accident into the thing on the poster, and we had both, without ever discussing it, drawn that line in the same place and promised ourselves privately we would die on the right side of it.

We did not die on the right side of it. We crossed it on a Tuesday, in our own bathroom, in the house we had bought from a photograph, and we crossed it together, and I am going to tell you the one thing about that day that I have never been able to make anyone on the outside understand, the thing Ruth cannot hear without her face going to pieces, the thing that is the whole reason I am writing this book instead of the one they wanted me to write.
I was not alone.

That is the thing. That is the only thing. On the worst day of my life, the day I became the thing I had sworn I would never become, I was not alone, because the person I loved most in the world was there, crossing the same line at the same moment, his hands shaking exactly as much as mine, and we looked at each other across that bathroom with a shame so total that there was, strangely, nothing left to hide, and in the ashes of all our pride there was this one thing standing, this one thing the fire couldn’t touch: we were still together. We had not let it make us lie to each other. We had not hidden it from each other, used behind each other’s backs, built the separate secret lives that it builds in everyone else, the lies that are the real thing that kills a marriage, worse than the drug. We had gone down into hell, but we had gone down holding hands, out loud, in front of each other, keeping nothing back, and I will tell you across nine years and his grave: that is not nothing. The world says it is nothing, the world says it is only two people destroying themselves, and the world is standing outside the bathroom door and cannot see that inside it there were two people who, even there, even then, at the absolute floor of their lives, refused to be alone in it. Refused to let even this be a thing they did apart.

I don’t expect you to agree with me. I expect you to be Ruth. But I was there and Ruth was not, and I am telling you what was in that room besides the horror, and it was love, it was our same stubborn thirty-year love, down there at the bottom with us, still holding on, still refusing to let go of the one hand it had held the whole way down.
After that, time changed shape, and I’ll tell it fast, because it went fast, because that is the other thing nobody warns you: the beginning takes years and the end takes months.

Our days, which had belonged to the work, began to belong to the clock. Not our clock — its clock. The day was no longer morning and afternoon and evening; it was the stretch after, when you were well and could almost pretend, and the longer stretch before, when the sickness started to come up again and the whole world narrowed to the one task of holding it off. We wrote less. Then we wrote badly. Then — and I made myself look at this, sober, later, it is the hardest page in the drawer — we wrote the pages that we could no longer tell were bad. The man behind the shoulder had not just been sent out of the room; the room itself was gone. There was no one left to tell us the work had stopped being good, because the part of us that knew good from bad was the same part that was now fully occupied, every waking hour, with the clock. The second books, both of them, the ones we had come to Alder to write, the ones the letter from New York had asked for — they stopped. Not dramatically. They just quietly stopped being written, the way a stream stops in a drought, no event, just less and less until one day you notice the bed is dry.
