I can give you the afternoon I understood it, because it had one, the way the good things had their afternoons. Daniel came into the kitchen at one o’clock with pages in his hand — the same hour, the same hand, as that August day with the three pages in the gold light. He gave them to me the old way. And I read them, and the life had gone out from under them: his rhythm was still there, the shape of his sentences was still there, but it was a man playing himself from memory, the bones of the thing with the warmth drained out. In August I had set his pages down unable to speak, and the silence had been the best thing I owned to give him. I set these down into the same silence, and we both heard what it meant this time, because by then we read each other’s silences the way you read weather — and this one did not mean it is that good. It meant it is gone. He took the pages back, gently. He did not ask me to say they were good. That was the one wall that never came down between us, in any of the fires: we did not lie to each other about the work, not ever, not even then, not even to spare each other the look on the other one’s face. So we didn’t. We stood in the ordinary one-o’clock light and let the truth be in the room with us — that the thing we had come to the end of the world to do, the thing we had wrecked our bodies and were selling our house to keep doing, had quietly stopped; and that, as with every good thing we ever had, we had not known the last day of it was the last day while we were standing in it.

The money went the way the writing went. First the savings, then the little that the first books still earned, then the things — I sold my grandmother’s ring, Daniel sold the first editions he’d spent his life finding, we sold the good car and drove a bad one, and then we started, slowly, to sell the house out from under ourselves, a room at a time, the way you’d burn the furniture to keep warm. The house we had bought from a photograph. The turret with the best window. All of it, going, to feed the one thing, and the terrible arithmetic of it was that it was never enough and never would be, because the floor kept dropping, because that is what the floor does.

And all around us, Alder was doing the same thing. That is the part the people far away never see, the part that made our private ruin feel less like a sin and more like weather. We were not freaks in a healthy town. We were one house on a street where it was happening in half the houses. The quiet patient line at the pharmacy that Daniel had joked about our first week — we understood it now; we were it. There were funerals. There were so many funerals that the one funeral home put in a second viewing room. The young men went first and then it stopped being only the young men. The church that had been for sale took itself off the market because it turned out there was work for a church after all, just not the work it had wanted. Grandmothers were raising their grandchildren up and down our road because the generation in the middle was gone or going. Alder had given the world coal for a hundred years, had sent its mountains away one trainload at a time to keep the country’s lights on, and when the coal was done the country had sent back, in exchange, this — the cheaper, nearer thing, the warmth carried one step too far down the road — and the town was dying of it with the same stubborn, uncomplaining, flinty grace it had done everything else. I loved Alder. I love it still. It is the only place that never once made me feel like a lesson. It was too busy being in it with me.

Ruth came. Of course Ruth came, the second winter, and she did not come gently — she had stopped being gentle, which was its own kind of love. She had done the reading and gathered the pamphlets and found the plain brick building three hours north and called them and learned what it cost, and she sat us down at our own kitchen table, the two of us on one side and her on the other, and she laid all of it out, the place and the beds and the money she would somehow find, and then she did the thing I had never once seen her do: she begged. Ruth is not a woman who begs. Daniel, she said, you are my brother, I have known you longer than she has — and she looked at me when she said it, not cruelly, only stating the plain arithmetic of a life — and I am watching you both die in this beautiful falling house, and there is a door, I have found the door, please, please walk through it.

And here is the thing she could not see, the thing that is the whole of this book. She thought she was looking at two people drowning, and she was right, we were. But she thought it meant we were each drowning, the way a person drowns, alone — that if she could only get us to the boat we would each, separately, be hauled out and saved. She could not see that we were not two people drowning. We were two people drowning together, holding on to each other in the water, and the holding-on was the one thing we had left that was still entirely ours, still unspoiled, still good — and that what she was asking, when she asked us to be saved, was to let go of each other and be saved one at a time, by strangers, on separate halls. She was offering to save our lives at the price of the only thing left in them we still wanted, and she did not know that was the price, because from where she sat there was no price at all. That is the whole distance between the inside of a thing and the outside of it, and I have never once, in all the years since, been able to carry a single person across it.

We said no. We said it kindly. We said the place sounded good and that we would think hard about it — which was the first lie either of us had told anyone in the whole long fall, and it was to her, to the one person trying hardest to save us, and I knew the moment it left my mouth that we had crossed something. The lying had never been part of it, not between us and not to the people who loved us. Now it had started, and it had started with Ruth, because that is exactly where the thing always makes you start: it knows, the way it knows everything, that the quickest way to keep you is to teach you to lie first to the ones who would take you from it. That was how I knew we were near the end — not by anything in our bodies, but by the lying, and by the way the ring had quietly closed down to just the three of us now, him and me and the thing, alone together in the falling house.
Here is Daniel, from the blue notebook, that same winter — a page I did not find until after, when his were the only voice left in the house.

I found this town. I want that written down in my own hand while I still have a hand that writes, because I can feel that coming too. I found the photograph. I turned the laptop around. I said look at this. Every road that led here, I was the one driving — the one on the map and the one in the rain, both of them — and I lie awake doing the sum a man in my position does at three in the morning, which is this: if I had not found Alder, if I had not been at the wheel, if I had not turned it away from the deer, she would be in the city tonight, whole, writing, afraid of nothing worse than a bad review. I did this to her. That is the sum. It is correct. There is no line in it I can cross out.

And then her hand comes across the gap in the dark — she is never as asleep as I think — and finds mine, and she says nothing, because she knows the sum as well as I do and knows there is no arguing me out of it at this hour. She just holds on. And the holding-on is her way of saying the one thing that is also true and that I can never quite believe at three in the morning and always believe again by light: that she is not a thing that was done to. That she came too. That by her own stubborn choice we are in this the same amount, exactly, down to the gram — and that the worst thing

I could do to her now, worse than the photograph, worse than the wheel, would be to decide up here alone in the dark, on her behalf, that she is only something I ruined. She will not let me keep that one. She reaches across every single night and takes it back out of my hand. I do not know what I ever did to earn being kept from my own worst arithmetic by a hand across a gap. But I did something, once, and it is the only thing I am sure I got all the way right.

And yet. I will set this down one time and never again, because a man should look at the worst thing in him at least once in his own hand. There is a kind of love that stays and holds the hand across the gap. And there may be another kind, a harder one I have never been strong enough for, that would find a way to take its hand away for good — so that the other one could finally climb out of the water, since climbing out together is the one thing we have proven, over and over, we cannot do. Some nights I think the most loving thing left in me is the one thing I am too much of a coward to do. Then the grey light comes, and she makes that small sound a sentence makes when it finally arrives in the next room, and I am so glad I am a coward that I could weep. But the thought has learned the way to the house now. It comes most nights. I let her hand be the thing that sends it home, and one day her hand will not be here, and I do not know what I will do then.
Daniel went first, the first time, on a night in the early spring, almost exactly two years after the oak tree.

I was in the next room. I want to be accurate: I was in the next room, writing, or holding a pen over paper, which was what writing had become. And the house was quiet in a way I had learned, without knowing I’d learned it, to be afraid of, and I went to find him, and he was in the bathroom, on the floor, and his lips were the wrong color and his skin was the wrong color and he was not making the sound a person makes, the sound you never notice until it stops, the small sound of a person breathing.

I knew what it was. Everyone in Alder knew what it was by then; the town had learned this the way other towns learn CPR. It is the quietest death there is. It does not thrash. The warmth that takes away pain and fear and grief takes away, at the end, if you ask it for too much, the body’s oldest instruction, the one that runs underneath everything, the one that says breathe — it just reaches down and switches off the breathing, gently, the way it switched off everything else, the way it switched off the fear and the critic and the pain, no drama, no struggle, the kindest killer there is. His body had simply, quietly, forgotten to breathe.

There was a kit in the house. By then there was a kit in every house in Alder, the little box with the spray in it that the county handed out at the library and the gas station and the church that was a church again, the thing that reaches in and tears the warmth off the lock, all at once, and gives the body back its oldest instruction. I had never used it. My hands knew how anyway; the town had taught us all, at kitchen tables, the way an older time taught people to deliver a baby or put out a chimney fire, because the help was fifty-one minutes away and you were the help. I used it. And I did the breathing for him, my mouth on my husband’s cold mouth on the bathroom floor of the house we were selling a room at a time, and I breathed for him until the thing in the spray reached the lock and tore the warmth off it, and he came back — he came back the terrible way they come back, all at once, sick and shaking and furious and alive, dragged up out of the kindest death and back into the ants and the dread and the cold tile, and the first thing he did, my gentle funny brilliant husband, the first thing he did on being hauled back from the dead, was weep, because I had brought him back into the one thing he had, for a few painless minutes, finally gotten to put down.

That is the night we decided to get clean. Not the next morning, when the resolve is cheap. That night, on the floor, both of us shaking, him weeping and me holding him and the little spent spray rolling away across the tile — that night, in the worst hour we had yet reached, we decided we were going to try to live. Together, the way we had done everything. We were going to go and get the thing torn off our locks on purpose, in a building made for it, and find out if there was anything left on the other side of the warmth, anything at all, that was worth staying for.

I didn’t know yet that the other side of the warmth was the hardest country we would ever cross. I didn’t know that getting the drug out of us would be worse than any day the drug had ever given us, that the body charges interest, that it keeps every drop of warmth it ever lent you in a ledger and calls the whole debt in at once. I didn’t know that the bravest thing Daniel ever did, braver than the accident, braver than the writing, would be to walk into that cold on purpose, holding my hand. And I didn’t know — how could I have known — that we would both make it through that cold, all the way through, to the dry ground on the far side, and that the cold would not be the thing that took him.
But that is the next part, and it is the hardest one to write, and I am not going to start it tonight.
THE JOY PLANT

Step out of the story again, and come forward — a long way forward from the Bat Cave, but still two hundred years back from us. England, the early part of the eighteen-hundreds. A world of coal smoke and horses and candlelight, of poets and consumption and long cold winters. And here is the thing you have to understand about that world to understand what happens in it: nobody knew. The idea that this flower could take hold of a person and not let go — the thing we now call addiction — had not yet been named or understood. And so the dried milk of the poppy, in a form called laudanum [LAW-duh-num], which is only the milk dissolved in alcohol, was sold openly, cheaply, legally, to anyone, in every kind of shop — by chemists, yes, but also by barbers and confectioners and grocers and the man who sold you your writing paper — and it was given for everything: for a cough, for a headache, for sleeplessness, for a sour stomach, for a crying child. It was the aspirin of its age, and more than the aspirin, and no one thought it any stranger than aspirin.

And a writer wrote it down. In 1821 a small brilliant ruined Englishman named Thomas De Quincey published a book with a title that told you exactly what it was: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater. He was the first person to write honestly, from the inside, about the whole of it — and the structure of his book is the thing I want you to see, because it is the structure of this one, written two hundred years before this one. He divided it into two parts. The first he called The Pleasures of Opium. And the second he called The Pains of Opium. He told, first, the truth almost no one will tell you — that it was wonderful, that it expanded the mind and sweetened the music and made the grey world glow, that he took “happiness,” he wrote, in liquid shape — and then he told the other truth, the nightmares, the ruin, the horror that came for the bill. The pleasures, and then the pains. In that order. Always in that order.

He was not alone. His friend Coleridge, one of the great poets of the language, dreamed the poem “Kubla Khan” whole, in an opium sleep, the images rising up before him, he said, “as things,” real as furniture — and woke and began to write it down, and got only a little way before a man knocked at the door, the famous “person from Porlock,” on business, and by the time Coleridge got back to the desk the rest of the dream had closed over like water, and the greatest poem he never finished stays a fragment to this day. And the same Coleridge wrote another poem, years later, out of the other half, out of the trying-to-stop, and called it “The Pains of Sleep,” and in it he wrote of a “soul-stifling shame.” The dreams, and then the shame. The pleasures, and then the pains. Two hundred years ago, by the best writers of their age, the whole of it already set down.

Clare and Daniel believed, that golden summer, that they had stumbled onto a private secret — that the warmth helped the work, that it opened the door the fear kept shut. They had stumbled onto nothing. They had walked into a room where the writers were already sitting, had been sitting for centuries, De Quincey and Coleridge and a long line of them stretching back and forward, every one of them having found the same door and written the same two chapters in the same order. There is nothing new under the warmth. There is only the pleasures, and then, always, in that order, the pains.
V. THE COLD
Ruth found the place, because Ruth found everything, and because by then we could not have found our own shoes.

It was a plain brick building three hours north, past the last of our mountains and out into the flat part of the state where the land gives up being beautiful and just gets on with being useful. Not one of the places you see in the magazines, with the horses and the infinity pool and the price that tells you the people there have something left to protect. This was the other kind, the kind for people who have nothing left, a county-and-charity place with linoleum floors and fluorescent light and a smell of institutional soap that I can still bring back behind my eyes, and I have never in my life been so grateful for an ugly building. Ruth paid what little it cost with money she did not have and has never once mentioned, and she drove us up there herself, the two of us in the back seat of her old car like children, sick already because we had made ourselves wait, holding hands, saying almost nothing, watching our mountains flatten out behind us.

And at the door they told us they would have to separate us. Men on one hall, women on another; that was the rule, it was a sensible rule, it was for everyone’s good. And I watched something happen to Daniel then that I had not seen through the whole long fall — not when the pills were cut off, not in the bathroom with the needle, not even on the floor coming back from the dead — I watched my husband, grey and shaking and barely able to stand, draw himself up to his full height and become, for one last time, the man who had stood up in a seminar room thirty years before and told a roomful of strangers that my one hidden sentence was the only honest thing in the story. He told them, quietly, that we had come this far together and we were not going to do this part apart; that if being apart was the price of their help we would turn around and go home and die in our own house, together, which was a real offer and they could hear that it was real; and that whatever they thought their rule was for, there was nothing they could protect us from in there that was worse than being alone in it.

They were good people. Overworked, underpaid, good people who had heard every kind of plea a sick person can make and had learned to say no to all of them. And they said yes to us. They bent their rule and they put us in a small room at the end of a hall with two narrow beds, side by side, and I want you to notice, because I did not notice until years later, that we ended as we had begun after the oak tree: in two narrow beds, side by side, in a room that was not ours, about to go through the worst thing a body can be asked to do, together.

I am going to tell you about the cold, now, because the author of my life owes it to you, and because everyone who tells these stories skips it or dresses it up, and it should be told once, plainly, by someone who was in it, so that you understand what it costs to come back, and so that you never again hear someone say they just need to want it enough without wanting to put your hand over that person’s mouth.
Here is what the body does when you finally take the warmth away.

Remember that the body had turned its own supply down, down, down, to match the flood. Remember that it stopped making its own, let its own locks rust, because why keep the lights on when the sun comes up in the kitchen drawer every morning. Now take the flood away. All at once, or near enough. And the body is left in a house where it has unscrewed every one of its own bulbs, in the dark, with no sun coming, and it panics, and it is a panic that has nowhere to go but out through every door the body has.

The ants came first, the way they had on that first Sunday, except now they did not stop. In the legs, in the arms, under the skin and then somehow under the bone, a crawling that no position could ease, so that Daniel and I lay in our two narrow beds and could not be still, could not stop moving our legs, kicking slowly at the sheets all night like two people running very slowly in their sleep toward something that never got closer. That is where the old ugly phrase comes from, the one people use lightly, kicking the habit — it is not a metaphor. You kick. For days. Your legs do it without you.

Then the cold, which is the thing it is named for, the deep true cold that has nothing to do with the temperature of the room, a cold that comes up out of the center of you as if the furnace that runs a human being had been let go out, so that you shake, not shiver, shake, your teeth going, your whole body clenched and juddering, and the sweat pouring off you at the same time, soaking the sheets, so that you are freezing and drenched at once and there is no blanket on earth that reaches it.

There is a name for this part older than any clinic, and it is as plain and as ugly as the thing it names. The skin goes into revolt. It pulls itself up into gooseflesh and will not come back down, hour after hour, every hair on your body standing on end, the skin crawling as though something were moving along underneath it, and you are cold the way meat is cold — and that is where the old light phrase comes from, the one people say when they mean they quit a thing all at once. Cold turkey. It is not a joke. It is a description. You lie there with the gray plucked gooseflesh of a cold bird on a counter, and you understand, somewhere far back behind the pain, that your own body has stopped being the place you live and become a thing that is happening to you.

And the body, having decided to empty itself, empties itself from every door it has, at once, for days. I am not going to dress this up, because dressing it up is the lie, and because the people who most need to hear it are the ones who believe this is a question of willpower. You are sick from both ends long past the point where there is anything left to give up, heaving over nothing, the body spending its last strength trying to turn itself inside out to flee a poison that is not in your stomach and never was — that is in the emptied lock of every cell, where no heaving can reach it. You foul yourself. There. I have written the thing that is in none of the movies. Two grown writers who had spent their lives agonizing over the right word lay in a clean bright room in their own sweat and filth, unable past a certain depth to get up in time, and unable past a certain depth to care, and dignity is the word the comfortable invented so they could look away from exactly this, and I am not going to let you look away from it, because it is true, and it happened to us, and we were not weak and we were not bad and it happened anyway.

And holding the whole of it open, underneath everything, is the sleeplessness. Not tiredness; there is no word small enough and none large enough. You do not sleep for days — not an hour, not ten minutes; the one mercy the body hands to every other suffering creature on earth is the one it withholds from you, precisely when you would trade your soul for it — and a mind held awake that long in that much pain begins to come apart along its seams. Time stops being a line and becomes a room you are locked inside, one endless unmoving three-in-the-morning, and the corners of the room begin to do things corners should not do, and you hear things moving in the pipes, and you know with a flat terrible clarity that you are losing your mind, and that there is no bottom to this, and that it has always been this way and always will be. That is the dread, the warmth turned all the way inside out — a horror with no object, a certainty pressing on every single cell that something unbearable is happening and will never stop. It is the body’s own grief for the thing it has lost, which it experiences, which it cannot help but experience, as the end of the world. And there is no sane watcher left anywhere inside you to lean down and say this will pass. Nothing in you believes it will pass. Every cell you own is certain, with a certainty that has nothing to do with thinking, that this is simply what being alive is now, that it is what you are owed, and that you brought it on yourself.

And it does not rise to a peak and break. That is the thing I need the comfortable to understand before anything else. It is not a bad night that a dawn ends. It is not even a bad week in the way a bad week keeps its worst day in the middle and eases after. It comes in waves with no crest, each one worse than the one before, for days without number, so that every hour you are certain you have finally struck the floor, the very worst a living body can be made to feel — and the next hour reaches calmly down past that floor and finds a lower room, and then a lower one. And the whole time, the entire time, there is a door. You know exactly where the door is. It is a phone call away and has always been a phone call away, and behind it now is not even heaven, not even pleasure — only the ants stopping, only the plucked skin lying back down, only permission, at last, to sleep — and the one thing you must do to open it is be weak for a single second, and the whole universe has narrowed to that door and that second, hour after hour after hour after hour. And the people outside, the comfortable ones, the ones who have never in their lives wanted anything the way every cell of your body is at that moment wanting this, say: they just need to want it enough. As if wanting were the thing you were short of. You have never wanted anything the way you want to open that door, and the not-opening of it, one second at a time, for days, with your mind coming apart and your body turning inside out and no sleep and no floor and no end you can believe in — that is the hardest and least-thanked thing a human being is ever asked to do, and most people cannot do it, and I have stopped, forever, thinking one inch less of the ones who cannot.
And we went through it three feet apart.

That is the part I have to make you feel, because it is the whole book again, here, at the bottom of the bottom. I lay in that cold and shook, and three feet away my husband lay in the same cold and shook, and we were both of us as low as a living body can go, stripped past dignity, past language some of those hours, two animals in a bright ugly room sweating and kicking and sick — and we could see each other. That is the thing. We were not alone in it. When the dread came up in me so hard that I made a sound I had never made before, I would feel, through the cold, his hand come across the gap between the beds and find mine, his hand shaking as hard as mine, no comfort in it in the ordinary sense, no warmth, two freezing shaking hands gripping each other in the dark — and it was everything. It was the difference between the two things it is possible to be in that cold. There is going through it alone, and there is going through it in the sight of the one person who loves you, who is in the identical cold, who looks at you across three feet of linoleum with their own eyes streaming — not weeping, your eyes simply stream in the cold, it is one of the body’s thousand doors thrown open, but it looks like weeping and after a while it becomes weeping because how could it not — and says nothing, because there is nothing to say, and does not look away. He did not look away from me, in the worst of it, and I did not look away from him, and I have come to believe that this, exactly this, two people refusing to look away from each other at the absolute floor of what a person can suffer, is as close as human beings are allowed to get to one another. Closer than the wedding. Closer than the good work. Closer than the warmth, which was only ever a counterfeit of this, the thing the god wears the face of. We did not hold each other through the cold because it felt good. Nothing felt good. We held each other through the cold so that neither of us would have to be the only one who had seen the bottom. And when it was over — and it does end, that is the one kindness, the body cannot keep it up forever, after some days the furnace relights and the ants recede and you sleep, finally, a terrible gray sleep, and wake emptied out and alive — when it was over, we had seen each other all the way to the bottom and all the way back, and there is no word in the language for what that does to a love. Ruth, who had never been to the bottom, called it codependency, later, when she was frightened for me. I have thought about her word for nine years. It is a good word, a careful clinical word, and it is standing a very long way outside the room.

Let me tell you the thing her word cannot reach, the thing I saw from inside the room that no word thrown from the hallway will ever touch. There was an hour — the third night, I think, though time had long since come loose — when I surfaced up out of my own sickness and looked across the gap and saw Daniel’s face while he did not know he was being seen. He had gone somewhere past knowing. And what I saw was not bravery and was not endurance; it was my husband afraid, purely, the way a small child is afraid, every mask a grown man wears burned off him, even the last one, even the one he had always kept on for me — and I understood that I was looking at the thing a person actually is under all of it, the small frightened animal at the very bottom of the self that we spend our whole lives dressing and hiding and keeping even from the ones we love most. I saw all the way down to his. And the gift of that ugly room, the gift I would not trade for a safe and separate life, is that at the same hour he was seeing all the way down to mine. We were each the only witness there will ever be to the other one’s absolute bottom. And having seen it — having seen the other with every last mask gone, and stayed, and not looked away, and not left — we never once after had to carry the question that every other human being carries quietly to the grave, which is whether they would still be loved if they were ever wholly seen. We had been wholly seen. We had stayed. You can call that codependency, if you are standing in the hallway. From inside the room it has another name, and the name is the whole of what two people are for.
I’ll give you the one hour I have never told anyone, because it is the floor under the floor, and if I am going to keep you in the cold with us you should see the true bottom of it.

It was the fourth night — or what I was still calling night, though the dark and the light had long since stopped meaning anything. We had been past speech for a long time by then. And somewhere in the worst of that hour a sound began to come out of Daniel that I had never heard from him in all our years, not in the car on the ridge, not on the bathroom floor — a low sound with no words in it, the sound a body makes when it has finally run out of every other thing it owns. And I lay three feet away and could not go to him. I could not get up. I could barely turn my head. I could only lie there and listen to the man I had loved my whole life make that sound into the dark, and I understood, for the first time, that there is a kind of suffering so far down that love cannot reach in and lift it out — that all love can do, at the very bottom, is be in the room.

So I did the only thing I had left. I turned my head the last few inches toward him, which cost me everything I had, and I made the sound back. I did not say his name; I had no name left in me, no words, nothing shaped. I only made the sound back, into the dark, so that his would not be the only one — so that whatever country he was lost in down there, he would hear that someone was in it with him, three feet away, making the same sound, and had not left. And after a while his hand came across the gap the way it always came, shaking as hard as mine, and found mine, and we lay there and made that sound back and forth to each other in the dark, like two animals calling across a distance, which is exactly what we were. It was the most human thing I have ever done. And the most human thing, I learned that night, is not a separate thing from the most animal thing; at the very bottom they are one thing, a living creature in the dark refusing to let another living creature be alone in the dark, and I have never since been able to tell the two of them apart, and I no longer try to.

Here is Daniel on it — not from the cold, because you cannot write in the cold, you cannot hold a pen or a thought in the cold — but from a week after, when his hand had steadied enough to try, in the blue notebook.

I have spent an hour hunting the words for the thing we just came through, and I have decided there are none, and that this is not a failure in me but a fact about the thing. Language was made by people sitting up — warm, fed, safe enough to want a name for a thing. It was not made for the floor of the cold. There is no word down there, because nobody who is down there has a word, and nobody who has a word is still down there. So all I can set down is this, and it is not a description, it is only a flag planted on a country I barely came back from: it was worse than dying. I have been near enough to dying now to set the two of them side by side, and dying was the kind one. Dying was warm. Dying came wearing Clare’s face. This was the other thing, the true opposite thing — every door the body has, thrown open at once onto winter. And the only reason I am sitting here on this side of it with a pen in my hand is that when I was all the way down at the bottom, with no word and no name and no self left in me, there was a sound in the dark three feet away, and the sound was Clare, making it back to me, and I put everything I had left into climbing up the sound until it turned, at the top, back into my wife.

We came home to Alder in the late spring, clean, into a house we had half sold and a life we had entirely wrecked, and I will tell you the truth about the far side of the warmth, because this is where the real courage was, and where almost nobody looks.

The withdrawal is the famous part. The withdrawal is in all the movies. But the withdrawal is only a week or two, and the body, as I said, cannot keep it up. The hard part, the part that takes the real and endless courage, is the gray that comes after, and stays, and stays. Because the body, which turned its own lights off, does not turn them back on just because you’ve suffered enough. It turns them back on slowly, grudgingly, over months, over the better part of a year, relearning how to make its own small warmth, its own drops, and until it does, you live in a world with the color drained out of it. Nothing is quite worth doing. Food is fuel. Music is noise that used to mean something. The things that once gave an ordinary person their ordinary daily reasons — a good meal, a joke, a morning, your wife’s face across a table — all of it comes to you through gray glass, at a distance, because the part of you that lights up at being alive has been unplugged and is being rebuilt one wire at a time, and no one can tell you how long, and some mornings you are absolutely certain it will never come back, that you have traded the warmth for nothing, for a gray forever, and that is the morning most people go back. Not in the cold. In the gray. The gray is what kills most of the ones who make it through the cold.

We did not go back. And I want to say clearly, because the whole shape of this book depends on it: those gray months, the hardest and least rewarded of our whole lives, the months of two emptied-out people relearning how to be alive in a half-empty house in a dying town — those months were also ours, also shared, and I do not rank them one inch below the golden summer when the words poured and the warmth lifted us like angels. I know how that sounds. Ruth would weep to hear it. But I have had nine years to weigh these things against each other, every kind of day we were given, and I have found that they do not weigh differently. The summer we wrote like gods and the winter we crossed a line in the bathroom and the week we shook in the cold and the long gray spring we sat at the table unable to feel the sun and got up the next morning and stayed anyway — I will not rank them. They were all us. They were all the one thing, which was a life, shared all the way down and all the way back, nothing held apart, nothing suffered alone. The people outside need there to have been good days and bad days, a honeymoon and a horror, so the story has a shape they can hold. I was inside, and from the inside there was only ever the two of us, going through whatever there was to go through, together. That is the thing I know that they don’t. That is the only thing I know that they don’t, and it is everything, and it is why I am not sorry, and it is why I can’t make them understand, and it is why, in the end, I stopped trying to make them and started trying, instead, to make them feel it, which is the only thing a book can do, which is why there is a book.

Slowly, the color came back. The body is faithful, in the end, even to people who have betrayed it; it relit its lights, drop by drop, through that summer, and one morning in August I bit into a peach on the back porch of our ruined house and it was so sweet and so cold and so entirely, violently there that I started to cry, standing up, holding a peach, because I had not tasted anything in a year and here, without any warning, was a peach, and the world had been in it the whole time, waiting, patient as the mountain, for me to be able to taste it again. Daniel came out to see what was wrong and I couldn’t explain, I just held out the peach, and he took a bite, and I watched it happen to him too, the same astonishment, the world coming back through the same door it had left by, and we stood on the porch of the house we had nearly died in and ate a peach and did not say one word, because some things are too large and too simple for words, and that was one of the good days, one of the best, right there at the end, and no warmth gave it to us. We had come back far enough to be given a peach. I did not know how few of those days were left.
We were clean for almost a year.

I need to tell you about that year, briefly, because it was quiet, and quiet years don’t get told, and this one should. We did not get our old life back — you don’t; the house was mostly gone, the money was gone, the second books were gone, the editor in New York had long since stopped writing. But we got a life back, a small careful one, built close to the ground. Daniel taught two days a week at the community college an hour away, and was, his students said, the best teacher they’d ever had, because a man who has been all the way to the bottom and climbed back has a certain thing to say to the young that the undamaged can’t fake. I started writing again — slowly, badly at first, the hand gone stiff, and then less badly — not the big book, something smaller and truer, about the town, about Alder, about the funerals and the grandmothers and the flinty grace of it. We went to the rooms, the meetings in the church basement, and sat in the folding chairs and held hands and did not say much, and it helped, the way it helps, by putting you in a room with people who know the thing you can’t explain to anyone else. We were, I think, happy, in the new gray-and-color way, the chastened way, the way of people who have spent everything and found, to their surprise, that there was something underneath the everything, something the fire hadn’t reached, and that it was enough.

I want to give you that year the way I gave you the first winter in Alder, because it was the last of the good, and because if you do not see it you will not understand what was taken. The people outside never see it. They see the before and the after and they skip the quiet middle, where two people were, against every odd, briefly, almost well.

Daniel teaching. I drove him the hour to the college those first months, because his license was gone and because I could not yet bear to let him out of my sight, and sometimes I sat in the back of the room pretending to read and watched him with those kids — nineteen, twenty, most of them the first in their families ever to sit in a college room, a lot of them from towns like Alder with the same thing eating the same houses. He did not teach them to write. He taught them that what they had to say was worth the trouble of saying well, which is the only thing anyone can really teach, and he taught it as a man who had lost everything and come back, so that when a boy who had never once been told his life was interesting read out three plain sentences about his father’s hands, Daniel went very still, and then said, quietly, that, keep that, that’s the good one — the same words, the exact words, he had said to me across a seminar table a lifetime before — and I watched the boy’s whole face change, and I had to look back down at my book. He was better that year than he had ever been at anything in his life. The damage had made him kind in a way the undamaged cannot counterfeit, and the kids knew it, and they lined up at his office door. One girl, who was in the thing herself, you could see it on her, used to come not for the writing but just to sit in his office for an hour a week and be in a room with an adult who had been where she was and gotten out. He never once rushed her. I have wondered since how many of them he saved in that one year, that he never knew he saved.

And I wrote. The small true book, about the town — at this desk, this one, where I am now. The sentences came slow and stiff at first, the hand gone cold after the years away, and then less stiff, and one afternoon I surfaced and understood that I had been writing for three hours and had not once thought about the thing, not once watched the clock, and I sat back and understood that the work had come back. Really come back. Clean this time, with no warmth under it and no cruel voice driving it out, just me and the page the way it had been over the dry cleaner thirty years before — and I put my face in my hands at this desk and cried, because I had believed that was gone forever, I had believed that was the price we paid, and here it was, handed back, for free, for nothing, for the single accomplishment of having stayed alive long enough to receive it.

And the meetings, the folding chairs in the basement of the church that had taken itself back off the market. I thought I would hate them; I am not a joiner, I spent my life outside rooms, watching them. But a thing happens in those rooms that happens nowhere else I have been, which is that every person in the circle already knows the one thing about you that you can never explain to anyone who hasn’t been where you’ve been — and so there is nothing to explain, and where the explaining would have been there is just, instead, company. An old miner named Virgil who had buried a son and found the thing in the boy’s room afterward and taken it up himself, at sixty, to be nearer to him — which is the saddest and most human reason I have ever heard, and which no one in that circle found strange. A young mother two years clean, white-knuckling it, holding her little coin like the last warm object on earth. Daniel and I did not say much. We held hands and we listened and we put our dollar in the basket and we drove home up the dark river road, and it was, I understand now, church — the realest church I was ever in, in a town where the bank had become one and nobody believed in anything except that they were all going to try not to die this week, together, which may be the only thing I have ever found that is actually worth believing in.
Here is Daniel, from that year — the last of the blue notebook but one. I keep it where I can reach it.

Second month clean and I can report that the world is the color of wet cardboard and food tastes like the idea of food and I would not go back for anything on this earth. That is the thing they never tell you — that you can be grey and half-dead and flat as a parking lot and still, underneath it, lower than the greyness reaches, know with total certainty that you would rather be here, awake, in the wet cardboard, with Clare in the next room making that small sound she makes when a sentence finally comes, than in any of the places the warmth ever took me. The warmth took me a lot of places. None of them had her in them. Not really. I only thought they did — that was the entire trick of the thing, it wore her face and I fell for it every single time. And now I am grey and clean and I can tell the difference again, and the difference is the one thing I know that is worth knowing: the warmth was her face on a stranger, and this — the wet cardboard, the real room, the real sound of her in it — this is her. I will take the wet cardboard. Every day of my life. I will take it.

That was the clean year, and I needed you to see it — to see that we made it back, that it was real, that we were, in the wet-cardboard way, in the chastened, grateful, holding-hands-in-the-basement way, happy — before I tell you how it ended, so that you will grieve it the way I grieve it: not as a tragedy that was always going to happen, but as a life, a good hard real life, that we had gotten back, that we were living, that was taken.

And through all of it, Daniel’s back went on speaking. That is the thing I come back to, lying awake even now. We had been given, by the oak tree, a pain with no end, an honest pain, a real one — and we had found the thing that ends all pain, and it had very nearly ended us, and we had crawled back from it across broken glass, and at the end of all of it, when everything else had been paid and lost and grieved and slowly, partly, mended — the back still hurt. Every single day. The first cause of everything, the honest reason, was still there, speaking, low and constant, the way it had spoken since the night in the rain, and it would speak every day for the rest of his life, and the thing that would quiet it in twenty minutes was a phone call away in a town where it was in half the houses, and he knew that, and I knew that, and we did not talk about it, and we held hands in the folding chairs, and we stayed.

We had one rule, by then. We had learned it in the cold and we never once said it out loud because it was too important to risk wearing out with words. The rule was the whole of what we had learned, the one thing the bottom had taught us, and it was this: not apart. Whatever came, whatever we did or didn’t do, whatever either of us reached for or put down, we would do it in the sight of the other one. We would not have secrets. We would not, ever again, be alone in anything. That was the rule, and it was not a rule about drugs, it was a rule about us, and it had carried us alive through every fire there was, and I believed in it the way you believe in the floor under your bed.

I was teaching myself, that whole quiet year, to believe we were going to be all right. I had almost managed it. That is where I have to stop tonight, with us almost all right, clean most of a year, eating peaches, holding hands in the church basement, Daniel teaching the young and me writing about the town, the back speaking its low word every day and the two of us staying anyway, together, under our one unspoken rule.

Because the next thing I have to tell you is the thing the whole book has been walking toward, the thing I have been turning my face away from for five parts, and it happened on an ordinary Thursday, and it happened because, for the first and only time in everything we ever went through, one of us was alone.
THE JOY PLANT

Step out one last time, into the making of our own world, and I will tell you the thing that I think, of everything in this book, you are least likely to already know, and least likely to forget once you do.

For two hundred years, every time we have made this flower stronger, we have sold the stronger thing as the cure for the weaker one. And every time, we have been believed, because the people doing the selling were not criminals in alleys. They were the doctors and the chemists and the great trusted companies of their day.

Start with the pure heart of it. Around the year 1804, a young German pharmacist’s apprentice named Sertürner [SER-toor-ner] did what nobody had managed before and pulled the one pure powerful thing out of the poppy’s milk — and it was ten times stronger than the milk it came from, and he named it, you remember, for the god of dreams. Morphine [MOR-feen]. A wonder. A gift. And then they invented, in the eighteen-fifties, a way to put it straight into the blood through a hollow needle, which made it faster and stronger still, and they gave it to wounded soldiers by the hundreds of thousands — in the American Civil War so many came home unable to stop that the thing nearly got a name of its own — and morphine, the wonder, began to show its other face.

So they went looking for a cure for the morphine. And in London, in 1874, a chemist boiled morphine with another chemical and made something stronger yet, and set it aside. And a great German company picked it up, and in 1898 they gave it a brand name — they took it from the German word for heroic, because of how mighty and well it made you feel — and they sold it, around the entire world, as a medicine, a cough syrup, a safe and non-addictive cure for morphine addiction. Heroin. The cure for the cure. It was in the catalogues. It was for children’s coughs. It took them years to admit what it was, and they only stopped selling it, and the law only caught up with it, after it had already gotten its hands into the century.

And here is the part that should stop your breath, because it is not history, it is us. In 1996, almost exactly a hundred years after Bayer, a company called Purdue brought out a new pill — stronger, longer-lasting, built from the same flower — and told the doctors of America, in their own printed materials, that “less than one percent” of patients who took it would become addicted. They had almost nothing to stand that number on; it leaned, in part, on a single short letter published in a medical journal in 1980, five words of which got quoted for thirty years, about hospital patients, a study that had nothing to do with their pill. But the doctors believed it, the way doctors had believed it about heroin, the way everyone always believes it, because why would the most trusted institutions of your age lie to you about medicine — and they wrote the prescriptions by the millions, and more than two hundred thousand Americans died of that pill alone, and when at last the pill was made harder to get, the people already caught in it turned, exactly as Daniel and I turned, to the cheaper nearer thing, and then to a thing stronger than any of it, made in warehouses, measured in grains too small to see, and the dying did not slow down. It sped up.

The same lie, every single time, for two hundred years. This new one is the safe one. Morphine is the safe opium. Heroin is the safe morphine. The pill is the safe heroin. And every time, the people who believed it were not weak and were not stupid. They were sick, and in pain, and they were told by the kindest and most trusted voices of their age that this time there was no shadow on it.

That is what Dr. Prewitt was told, in his training, by his journals, by the companies’ smiling men who brought the lunch. And that is what Dr. Prewitt, who was kind, who was tired, who had a waiting room full of hurting people, told Daniel and me, in his brown office, and in the sunny kitchen, over the windowsill, in good faith, every word of it meant as mercy. Everyone was kind. There was no villain. There is never, quite, a villain. There is only the lie, the oldest and most reasonable lie there is, told again and again down the centuries in the voice of medicine itself — and underneath the lie, unchanged in ten thousand years, patient as the Bat Cave, the flower, which takes away pain and fear and grief exactly as it always has, and which does not lie, and has never once needed to.
VI. HOME AGAIN
The thing that took him, in the end, was a good thing. I have had to learn to hold that, and it is the heaviest of all of them.

That autumn — our second clean autumn, almost a year dry — a small magazine took the first piece of the thing I’d been writing about Alder, the quiet true thing, the funerals and the grandmothers and the flinty grace, and then a little festival two hours south, in the college town, asked if I would come and read it. It was nothing. It was a church hall and forty folding chairs and a check that barely covered the gas. But it was the first time in six years that the world had asked either of us to come and be a writer, out loud, in front of people, and Daniel would not hear of my saying no. His back was bad that week — the cold had come early and the cold always woke the metal and the deep torn place — and the drive would have been two hours each way on hard seats, and he could not have borne it, and we both knew it, and so we did the thing we had not done in all the years of the fire: we decided I would go alone, and come home the next morning. One night. He all but pushed me out the door. He stood on the porch of our half-sold house in his old cardigan and watched me back the bad car down the drive, and he was smiling, and the last thing he said to me, calling it down the drive, was go be a writer, Clare, somebody in this house should, and he was laughing when he said it, and I was laughing, and that is the last thing, that is the last whole thing I have of him, my husband laughing on the porch in the cold, proud of me, sending me off to be the thing we had come to the end of the world to be.

I read the piece. People were kind. A young woman came up afterward with my first book, my old one, the one the reviews had called promising, and asked me to sign it, and told me it had meant something to her in college, and I stood in a church hall two hours from home and felt, for one evening, like a person who had a life. I called Daniel that night from the motel. He was tired and his back was bad and he was glad for me, I could hear it, and we talked for a while about nothing, about the young woman and the book, and he told me to sleep well, and I told him to take his medicine for the back — the real medicine, the allowed kind, the small careful kind

— and go to bed, and he said he would, and we said the thing we always said, the ordinary thing, and I hung up, and I slept well, in a motel, two hours away, for the first and only night in everything we ever went through that I was not in the next bed.

I have spent nine years not knowing what happened in our house that night, because the one person who could have told me was alone. That is the particular cruelty of it, the one that is mine to carry: everything else we did, we did in each other’s sight, and so I have it, all of it, every fire, witnessed, shared, mine as much as his. But the last hours of his life happened with no one there, and so they are the one part of our whole life together that I do not have, that I will never have, that I can only build out of what I know and then take apart again at three in the morning and build again. I know the back was bad. I know the house was empty in a way it had not been empty in thirty years of marriage. I know that the thing that quiets a screaming back in twenty minutes was, that autumn, in half the houses in Alder, a phone call away, and that he knew exactly where, and that he had known, every single day for a year, and had stayed, because I was there, because of the rule, because we were not apart. And I know that on the one night we were apart, with the pain up and the house silent and no one’s eyes to meet across the gap, he reached back. Just once. I believe it was just once. I believe, I have to believe, I have built my ability to go on living on believing, that it was not a decision, not a door he chose, just a man alone with an old honest pain reaching for the only thing that had ever fully answered it, the way you’d reach in the dark for a hand that had always been there.

That is the version I told myself for nine years, and I told it so well and so long that I could nearly hear it in his voice — which, you will understand before this book is finished, is a thing I have learned to do. I am not going to leave it standing. I have laid that night out in a row, the way I once laid the cracks of the first autumn in a row, and the pieces do not say what I made them say. They say something worse. But let me do it in order, the way I have done all of it. Let me give you his last page first, the way I have given you everything of his, and then I will tell you the truth about the last page, because the truth about the last page is the truth about the whole of it, and you have earned it by now, and so, God help me, have I.

And his body had forgotten. That is the mechanical heart of it, the part with no mercy and no meaning in it at all. A year clean, his body had done the faithful thing, had turned its own locks back on, had rebuilt its tolerance down to nothing, down to a baby’s — which is the whole point, which is the body healing, which is the reward for all that cold. So the amount that a year before had been a Tuesday, had been nothing, had been just enough to get back to ordinary — that amount, in a body that had healed, in a body that had forgotten how to survive it, was a flood where now there were only drops. And the warmth did the last thing it does, the kindest and the worst, the thing it had tried once before on the bathroom floor when I was there to breathe for him. It reached down into my husband, alone in our house, and switched off the oldest instruction, gently, with no drama, and this time there was no one in the next room to hear the sound stop, and no one to find the little box the county gave out, and no one to put her mouth on his mouth and breathe. He had made it all the way through the cold. He had made it all the way across to the dry ground. And then, on the one night he was alone, the healing killed him.

And here is the piece of that I could not pick up for nine years either, because it will not be put down once you have it: he knew. He had sat in the same church basements I had and heard the same flat warning they save for the end of the meeting, the one about the clean body and the old number, about how the thing that healed you is the thing that makes the old amount a killing amount. He knew better than almost anyone alive what a year of staying clean does to the arithmetic. A man who reaches, after a year, for the number that used to be a Tuesday is not a man who forgot. He is a man who remembered.

Here is Daniel. The last page of the blue notebook. Written that night, I think — the ink is the pen we kept by the chair in the parlor — and it is not about any of what I have just told you, because he did not know, when he wrote it, that there was anything to tell. It is just an ordinary page, the last ordinary page, and that is why I can hardly bear to copy it out, and why it is the truest thing in this whole book, and why I am going to end his part of it here, on his own words, where it belongs.

Clare gone to read. The house too quiet. I keep waiting to hear her in the next room and she is not in the next room, and I find I don’t know what to do with a quiet I can’t turn and talk into. Thirty years and I have never learned to be in a room she isn’t in. I hope they were kind to her tonight. They’d better have been. She stood up in a seminar room half my life ago with a sentence she was ashamed of, and it was the best thing in the room, and I knew it before she did, and tonight a church full of strangers two hours away is finding out the thing I have known since I was twenty-nine, which is that I married the real one. I was always the one they called promising. She was the one who was good. I figured that out years ago and decided to love her instead of mind it, which is the single smartest thing I have ever done.

The back is loud tonight. I’ll take the allowed thing and put myself to bed and she’ll be home by noon and I’ll make her tell me every word of it twice. We have almost nothing left, the house is half gone, we are two broke wrecked old writers in a dying town, and I lay here tonight and did the thing you’re not supposed to be able to do anymore, I counted up what we have, and I’ll tell you, notebook, since you’re the only one awake: it comes out higher than it has any right to. We went all the way down and we did it holding hands. Not one thing in thirty years did I have to go through by myself. Do you know how few people get to say that. I’d do the whole thing again. The oak tree and the warmth and the cold and all of it, every second, if the alternative was doing it alone, or worse, having her do any of it alone. I’d sign for the whole ruin again tomorrow, happily, for the single fact of having been in it with her the whole way.
She’ll be home by noon. I can almost stand the quiet if I know she’ll be home by noon.
Goodnight, Clare. Come home.

I came home by noon. I want to say that, because he wanted me home by noon, and I was. I came up the drive a little after twelve with the reading still warm in me and a signed copy of my own old book on the seat, ready to tell him every word of it twice, and the house had the wrong feeling before I was out of the car, the quiet I had taught myself to be afraid of, and I will not tell you about the finding, I have told you everything else but I will not tell you that, it is the one thing I am keeping, an old woman is allowed to keep one thing. I will only tell you that he was in his chair in the parlor, in the colored light, which had moved across the floor all morning the way it does, across him, and that the blue notebook lay open on the floor beside the chair where it had gone from his hand, and that it was many hours too late, and that there was no breath to bring back, and that the little box the county gives out was in the kitchen drawer where it had always been, unopened, three rooms away, useless, because the whole terrible science of it is that the box only works if someone is there, and for the first time in thirty years, no one was there.

Ruth came. The town came. There were so many funerals in Alder by then that they knew exactly how to do it, which is its own unbearable thing, a town so practiced at burying its own that it moves through the motions with a terrible gentle competence, the casseroles already made, the second viewing room already open. The people held my hands in both of theirs, the way they do, and looked at me the way you look at the lesson at the end of a story, and I let them, because they were kind, and because there was no way to tell them, standing in the funeral home, that they had the story wrong, that it was not the story they thought, that I would not be standing there in the one thing I had that was black if I had been willing, thirty years ago, to be a person who went through her life alone and safe.

And Ruth — Ruth who had been right about everything, Ruth who had begged and researched and found the ugly blessed building and driven us there herself — Ruth held me longest, at the end, when the others had gone, and she said the thing she had been not-saying for years, she said, if you had just, and she couldn’t finish it, and she didn’t have to, because I had a thousand ways to finish it myself. If you had just listened sooner. If you had just let me take him when he’d have let himself be taken. If you had just not gone to that reading. If you had just been in the next room, one more night, the way you were every other night for thirty years, you could have breathed for him, you had done it before, you knew how, the whole town knew how, you could have brought him back.

She didn’t say that last one. And for nine years I let it be the shape of the whole thing — my fault, my one night away, my broken rule. I wore it the way I wore the black dress. It was easier to be the woman who left than to be the woman who knows what I am about to tell you, because guilt at least keeps the dead innocent, and I wanted him innocent more than I wanted the truth.

But I have laid that night in a row, and the pieces do not say what I let them say. Here are the pieces. For nine years he had turned down every reason to leave that house without me — every reading, every doctor two counties off, every trip Ruth ever tried to put him on — and then, that one autumn, he insisted, he all but carried me to the car, for a church hall and forty folding chairs he could not otherwise have cared less about. His back was bad that week; his back was bad every week; it had been bad for nine years and had never once sent me away before. He knew exactly where the thing was, and had known every single day for a year, and in all that year, with it a phone call away, he never once reached for it — not while I was in the house. And on the one night I was not, he did. The rule we had kept like a religion for thirty years, the not-apart that had carried us through every fire, he did not break by accident on the single worst possible night of all the nights there were. He chose the night. He made the night. He sent me two hours down the road to feel like a writer so that I would be two hours down the road when it happened.

He did it so that it would not be me. That is the piece I could not pick up, and it is the whole of it. Not so no one could stop him, though no one could. So that it would not be me who found him breathing wrong and had to decide, one more time, whether to drag him back into a life he could no longer carry; so that I would be in a bright hall being a person instead of on a bathroom floor with my mouth on his; so that the last thing he did to me was not one more thing I had to survive him doing. He had come to believe, somewhere in that long quiet autumn, that there was nothing left he could give me but his absence — that as long as he was in the room for me to hold on to, I would hold on, and we would go on holding each other down in the warm dark we had made, the two of us the reason neither of us could ever climb all the way out. And he decided to be the one who let go of the hand. He thought it was the last kindness he had in him.

And I will not call it that. I have had nine years and I will not. He thought it was love and it was not love; it was the warmth, at the very end, telling him in his own gentle reasonable voice that the loving thing was to go — and that was the last lie it ever told him, and the cruelest, because the loving thing was to stay. To be broken and boring and alive in the next room. To let me have him ruined for forty more years rather than not have him at all, and to let me be the one who decided what I could carry. He took that from me. He decided, alone, in the dark, that my life would be better with him gone out of it, and then he arranged it so that I could never once argue the point, and there is a word for a man who loves you and leaves you certain it was for your own good, and the word is not kindness. He had no right. I do not forgive him for it. I understand it all the way to the bottom, which is worse than not understanding it, and I still do not forgive him, and I have stopped trying to, because the not-forgiving is the last argument he and I are ever going to have, and I am not ready to let him win it by being dead.
There is one more thing, and it is the hardest, and I have kept it for the end because once you have read it you cannot read the rest of this book the way you read it the first time.

I told you, at the very start, that I was writing this out of both of us — me now, at the desk, and Daniel then, in the blue notebook, in his own words, which were always better than mine. That was true of every page but one.

When I came up the drive that noon, the blue notebook lay open on the floor by the chair, face up, where it had gone from his hand. I have told you I will not describe the finding, and I am keeping that. But I will tell you the one thing I have never told a living soul, which is that the page it lay open to was blank. The last page. He had taken down the pen we kept by the chair, the way he had ten thousand nights of his life, the man who did not believe a thing had happened to him until he had written it — and he had written nothing. Not a line. Not a word. Not the worst sentence of the day. On the one night of his whole life that he was alone, he left the page white, and a blank page from Daniel was not nothing. It was the loudest page in the house. It was the thing I have just spent a chapter telling you, set down in the one language he knew I would have to read: the silence of a man who has decided a thing he cannot write where his wife will find it.

And I could not bear it. I have to ask you to hold two things that will not sit together — that I was not in my right mind that week, which no one is, and that I knew exactly what I was doing. I could not bear that his last night was wordless, and I could not bear what the blank page was saying, and so I did the thing I did. That week, at this desk, with his pen, in the downhill hand I had been forging for thirty years as a joke and could have done in my sleep, I wrote the last page of the blue notebook. The one you read. The seminar room and the real one and the smartest thing he ever did. The counting-up of a ruined life. I’d sign for the whole ruin again. Goodnight, Clare. Come home. Every word of it is mine. He never wrote a line of it. I gave my dead husband the last page he did not leave, because I would not live in a house where his last night was blank, and because I would not — I will not, even now, even here — let the thing that killed him have the final word in his own voice.

And here is what I did with it, and it is the truest thing I know about myself and the worst. I took the warm page and I laid it down over the cold one. What I believe is that he counted up our whole life that night and found that it was the thing killing us both — the madness we had kept warm between us all those years, the holding-on that was also a holding-down — and that he stepped out of the room to end it. What I wrote is a man who counted up the same life and found it worth every second and lay down meaning to wake. I wrote him choosing us. I buried the thing I think actually took him — the thing this book is named for — under a loving page in his own hand, on purpose, with my eyes open, because I would rather forge my husband’s love than report his despair, and I would do it again tonight.

I do not know which of them is the real one — the Daniel I think let go of my hand to save me, or the Daniel I wrote who would never have let go at all. I have decided to believe the one I wrote. I am telling you plainly that it is a decision and not a fact, so that you do not close this book and take my mercy for the truth; but I have made it, and I will make it again every morning I have left. I became, at the very end, the thing the young pharmacist named the drug for two hundred years ago, the thing Daniel told me about across a kitchen table in the gold light, lit up and delighted and not knowing he was naming the end of us: the one who comes to you in the night wearing the face of someone you love, and gives you, in their own voice, the one thing you cannot go on living without having heard. I came to Daniel. I put on his face. I wrote him home.
So now you know why I cannot say it the way Ruth needs me to say it, and why I also cannot say it the way the world needs me to say it, and why it took a whole book.

If you asked me — would you undo it — I would say yes, instantly, without one second’s thought. I would undo the oak tree. I would make the doe step out one minute later. I would take the pain and the amber bottle and the needle and the cold and the gray and the peach and the church basement and the chair in the colored light, all of it, every second, and I would give it all back in a heartbeat to have Daniel old and whole and boring beside me, two writers who never had an accident, who wrote their forgettable second books and grew dull and gray together and died in some ordinary far-off way with the lights on and someone in the next room. I would trade our whole blazing ruin for that gray safe nothing in less time than it takes to say so, and anyone who tells you different about their own lost love is performing. I am not performing. Given the choice, I would undo all of it. The drug was never worth anything. It took everything, and it gave nothing back that it did not first steal, and it killed the best man I ever knew, alone, three rooms from the thing that could have saved him. Let no one close this book thinking I said the warmth was worth it. The warmth was a counterfeit and a thief and I would burn every poppy on earth to have him back.

But I was not given the choice. That is the thing. Nobody is. The oak tree happened, and the pain was real, and the mercy was real, and the door closed the way it closes on everyone, with no click, and once we were inside the thing we could not undo — once it was simply the terrain of our life, the mountain we happened to live on, the weather we happened to get — then the only question left, the only question any of us ever really gets, was how. Not whether. How. And the how was the one thing that was ours, the one thing the drug could not take, the one thing I would not trade and will not let Ruth or the world or you take from me now: we went through it together. All of it. Every inch of the thing we could not undo, we went through in each other’s sight, holding hands, hiding nothing, alone in nothing — the joy and the work and the warmth and the line in the bathroom and the cold and the gray and the peach, none of it ranked, none of it suffered by one of us out of the sight of the other, one whole human catastrophe lived all the way down and all the way back by two people who refused, to the very last night, to be alone in it. And that — not the drug, never the drug — is the thing I wrote that Daniel counted up on his last night. Whether he truly counted it that way, or whether I counted it for him and forged his name under it because I could not stand the sum he actually reached, it is the one figure I am certain of, and I will sign it in my own hand, awake and sober and in the daylight where it can be checked: it was never the warmth that was worth anything. If a single thing in our life was worth what it cost us, it was the hand across the gap, and nothing else, and I would sign for that on any page you put in front of me. So I am signing. The ruin I would undo in a heartbeat. The togetherness inside the ruin I would not trade for a safe and separate century. Both of those are true, and holding them both at once, without dropping either, is the whole of what I have, and it has taken me nine years and this entire book to learn to carry it, and I think, tonight, finally, I can.
There are two stacks of notebooks on the desk in front of me, and one of them is still his.

I have been writing out of both of us, because it was the only honest way, and because the second book, the one that would not come, the one we drove to the end of the world to write and then could not write because the thing that unblocked us was the same thing that was unmaking us — it turns out it was this one, all along. It was always going to be this one. It just had to wait until one of us was left to write it, clean, at the old desk, in the colored light, with his voice still in the blue notebook saying come home.

I’m home, Daniel. I came home by noon. I’ve been home nine years. And I have finally written the thing you always said I was the one who could write, and it is about you, and it is about us, and it is the truest thing I have ever done, and I did it alone, which is the one way I never wanted to do anything, and which is, I have come to think, the last gift the two of us had left to give each other: that one of us lived to tell it, so that it would not, in the end, go untold, the way your last night went — unwitnessed, alone, in a quiet house, with the light moving across the floor.

Not this. This last one, at least, we made the way we made everything — you on your pages for as long as you had pages to write, and me on mine, and then, at the end, me on yours, in your hand, giving you the words you did not leave. It is the only way there is left to do a thing together with the dead. It is a kind of not-apart. It is the last kind I get.
Goodnight, Clare. Come home, I wrote, in your hand, on the blank page, because you did not.

So I will answer the page I wrote. I came home, Daniel. I came home by noon, the way you told me to — the way I told you to tell me. I’ve been home nine years. And I have written us all the way to the end now, the true and the forged laid down in the same ink, where no one can ever pull the one back out of the other, and I am going to close the blue notebook, and close mine, and let you sleep the way I have decided you slept: counting us up, and finding us worth it, and meaning to wake.
Goodnight, Daniel. I’m home.
WHAT IT DID
Set down plainly, the way a field-worker records what was in front of them, this is what the substance did in this book.

What it was. Heroin, and before it the medicine it is descended from, and before that the poppy they are both drawn from. A relief drug: it works on the body’s own system for switching off pain, fear and want, and it opens that system all the way.

Time. It did not so much speed time or slow it as empty it of weight. Whole afternoons passed without being spent. The day stopped being morning and evening and became the short stretch after and the long stretch before.

The body. First the end of pain — not pain reduced but pain deposed, still there and governing nothing. Then the body, finding the flood arrive every day, turned its own supply down to meet it, so that in time the drug no longer lifted anyone to heaven; it only returned them to ordinary, and ordinary could be reached no other way.

The self. The whole anxious committee that runs a person — the one that keeps the accounts, remembers the failures, stands behind the shoulder and says you are a fraud — fell silent. What was left, the first time, felt like peace, and like being held by something that wanted nothing. It was the most dangerous gift either of them was ever given, because it came wearing the face of everything they loved.

The world. For one season the work came as it never had, and they believed the warmth had opened the door the fear kept shut. The pages they kept prove the work was real. They also show that the door it came through was the same door that was closing on everything else.

What it meant.
