That the deepest closeness two people can reach and the thing that destroys them can arrive together — through one door, in one warmth, wearing one beloved face — and that no one, however clear-eyed, can take the one without the other. That is not a weakness in the people it happened to. It is the design of the thing.

The cost. It took the work, the money, the house, and the years. It took the body’s own ability to make its small daily peace, and gave nothing lasting back for it. And on the night the body had healed enough to be killed by the old amount, it took the better of the two, alone, three rooms from the thing that could have saved him. It lets fewer people back out than any door in this series. It is still, as these words are set down, killing more each year than the year before.
THE MAPMAKER
For Candace Pert, and for Friedrich Sertürner.

Two people drew the map of this one, at the opposite ends of its long story — one at the beginning, who pulled the drug out of the flower, and one near the end, who found the lock in us that the drug had been looking for all along.

In a pharmacy in a small German town, around the year 1804, a pharmacist’s apprentice barely out of his teens named Friedrich Sertürner [SER-toor-ner] did a thing no one had managed in all the thousands of years people had used the poppy: he drew the single pure, powerful thing out of its milk — the white crystal at the heart of it that does the work. It was the first time anyone had pulled the active substance out of any plant at all, the small beginning of the science that now gives us nearly every medicine we have. He tested it on himself and on three boys, none of them older than seventeen, and very nearly killed them all finding out how strong it was. And he gave it a name. He was young, and it was an age of poets, so he reached for the oldest story he knew and named his white crystal after Morpheus [MOR-fee-us], the Greek god of dreams — the one who slips into a sleeper’s room at night wearing the face of someone the sleeper loves. He called it morphium, a name the world would soon smooth to morphine. He could not have named it better if he had known everything that was coming.

A hundred and seventy years later, and an ocean away, a graduate student named Candace Pert [kan-DASS PURT] answered the question Sertürner’s crystal had left hanging in the air: why should the human brain have any use at all for a chemical squeezed out of a flower? In 1973, in a laboratory at Johns Hopkins, working under Solomon Snyder, she proved that the brain carries a lock the drug fits — a receptor [ree-SEP-ter], a keyhole shaped, it would turn out, for the body’s own painkillers, the faint daily relief we make in small amounts for ourselves and call endorphins [en-DOR-fins]. The poppy had spent ten thousand years quietly picking a lock every one of us is born carrying. She was twenty-six years old. A few years on, when the field’s great prize was given for the work and her name was left off it, she said so, out loud, which was not the done thing and cost her something, and which this page records because the truth of who did the work is the whole reason the page exists. She spent the rest of her life on the chemistry of feeling, and died in 2013.

Neither of them is honoured here for what the drug became. They are honoured for seeing clearly — one into a flower, one into us — and for the plain fact that we know what this thing is because they stopped and looked.

Sources. Sertürner isolated morphine from opium in 1804 — the first alkaloid ever drawn from a plant — and named it morphium, later smoothed to morphine, for Morpheus; his full account and near-fatal self-experiment with three boys were published in 1817 (he lived 1783–1841). Pert’s demonstration of the opiate receptor: C. B. Pert and S. H. Snyder, “Opiate Receptor: Demonstration in Nervous Tissue,” Science 179 (March 1973). The brain’s own opioids, the enkephalins: Hughes, Kosterlitz and colleagues, 1975. The 1978 Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award, given for this work to Snyder, Hughes and Kosterlitz, passed over Pert, who protested her exclusion. C. Pert, Molecules of Emotion (1997).

GLOSSARY
endorphin [en-DOR-fin] — a shortening of endogenous morphine.
The body’s own faint, daily painkillers, made in small amounts; the poppy’s drugs are flooded copies of them.
hul gil [hool GEEL] — Sumerian, joy plant. The poppy’s name on the oldest written tablets we have.
laudanum [LAW-duh-num] — apothecary Latin. Opium dissolved in alcohol; sold openly and cheaply for almost any ailment through the eighteen-hundreds.
Morpheus [MOR-fee-us] — The Greek god of dreams, who slips into a sleeper’s room at night wearing the face of someone the sleeper loves.
morphine [MOR-feen] — named for Morpheus. The first pure drug drawn out of the poppy, isolated about 1804; many times the strength of the milk it came from.
nepenthe [neh-PEN-thee] — Greek, no-grief. In Homer, a drug slipped into wine that takes away grief and the memory of pain.
opion [OP-ee-on] — Greek, the juice. The white milk wept by the scored poppy; the root of the word opium.
Pert, Candace [kan-DASS PURT] — The American scientist who, in
1973, proved the brain carries the lock the poppy’s drugs fit.
receptor [ree-SEP-ter] — The lock, or keyhole, on a brain cell that one particular chemical fits; the poppy’s drugs fit the one the body keeps for its own painkillers.
Sertürner, Friedrich [SER-toor-ner] — The German apothecary’s apprentice who first drew morphine out of the poppy and named it for the god of dreams.
